speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity that I am being given today to focus attention on International Human Rights Day. This event is of particular importance at a time when, more than ever, the peoples of the five continents have legitimate aspirations to freedom, social justice and the rule of law.
Today we commemorate the 43rd anniversary of the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on December 10, 1948. The world has changed radically since then. Considerable progress has been made in many areas, especially on the world political scene.
In the past two years alone, we have seen the tearing down of the Berlin Wall, which symbolized the cold war, and revolutionary changes throughout eastern Europe. The improvement in east-west relations has had a ripple effect: the reunification of the two Germanies and the holding of free elections in eastern bloc countries are impressive testimony to this.
The Communist regimes of eastern Europe have collapsed under the pressure of the democratic aspirations of peoples too long deprived of their individual and political freedoms. In Africa, several countries including Benin, Ivory Coast, Zambia and Namibia have chosen the path of democracy.

In South Africa the apartheid system is being dismantled. In Asia elections have been held in countries such as Mongolia and the Philippines and at last the end of the rivalry between the two major blocs has enabled the United Nations to revive the co-operative spirit of the charter. The UN has regained its decisive role in maintaining international order and in seeking to resolve conflicts.
This new climate of co-operation and this emerging new world order along with disarmament talks have allowed a redefinition of the concept of security based on socio-economics far more than on military foundations.
Our concept of security must now be adapted to suit a new environment that includes all threats to global peace and stability.
Chronic poverty, debt, socio-economic disparities, destruction of the environment, unresolved regional conflicts, governments with repressive regime, all these socio-economic pressures represent threats to world peace and call for international joint action and ongoing political dialogue among all countries. A better understanding of the human factor and recognition of the universality of such fundamental values as individual and political freedom are essential to the advancement of all the world's societies.

Respect for human rights and the maintenance of peace and security are closely related, as are freedom and human development.
Our own country's security is also closely tied to our openness to the world and our desire to build a united Canada with democratic, economic and cultural freedom, a Canada that is proud to promote its values and convictions beyond its borders, a Canada that will play a leading role on the international scene in the 21st century.

December 10, 1991
Routine Proceedings
The promotion of human rights has been one of the cornerstones of Canada's foreign policy for several years and is manifested in various types of activities. These include: our support for international institutions such as the United Nations Commission on Human Rights; our policies in favour of human rights and democratic development in our bilateral relations; our material and technical assistance to countries and institutions to support the promotion of human rights; the creation of an International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development; Elections Canada's support to the electoral process; and our development assistance program.
Canada's membership in international institutions such as the Commonwealth and La Francophonie consi-tutes a decisive factor in the quality and credibility of our political dialogue with other countries.
Canada's influence on the international scene is increasingly effective in efforts to achieve greater respect for human rights. The growing credibility that we have acquired beyond our borders stems from the quality of our activities and the vision that we seek to share with all human societies. Under the remarkable leadership of the Prime Minister, Canada has distinguished itself by its firm positions and innovative initiatives.
At the closing of the Dakar Summit in 1989, the participants issued a joint statement calling for respect for human rights and for the right to development. This statement, proposed by Canada, clearly defined the link between individual rights and the rights of peoples.
At the World Summit for Children, held in New York in September 1990 under the co-chairmanship of the Prime Minister of Canada, not only did Canada play a very active role, but we have also honoured our commitments through concrete initiatives, including our important financial support to the universel immunization program.
At the Commonwealth Summit in Harare last October, the issue of human rights was raised at Canada's urging. Canada played a leading role, as well, in the decision not to hold the fourth Francophone summit in Kinshasa, in the presence of Colonel Mobutu. The summit was moved to Paris.
I think that I must also mention Canada's support to Haiti's only legitimate leader, President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, who is in our country right now and whom I will have the pleasure of welcoming to Ottawa in a few minutes.
And yesterday, Canada suspended approval of new aid projects to Indonesia as a sign of indignation following the recent killings in East Timor and to reflect our concern about the human rights situation in this country.
Finally, the Prime Minsiter of Canada's firm position on human rights and democratic development set the tone for discussion and for the final declaration of Chaillot. Let me quote the key passage:
Gathered to reaffirm our solidarity and our firm desire to work together actively to shape a better future for our peoples and for the international community- we, the heads of state, government and delegations gathered at Chaillot thus intend to live up to our historic responsibilities and to respond to the legitimate aspirations of our peoples in a new international context.
This new international context is sending us clear messages that call for a shared concept of the rights and freedoms associated with human development.
The whole world is moving irreversibly toward greater respect for human rights and freedoms.
This movement is based on growing awareness of our interdependence and our common destiny and on a broadly shared desire for global development that is both democratic and sustainable.
Mr. Speaker, 43 years ago in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights the peoples of the United Nations proclaimed their faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person and in the equal rights of men and women, and determined to promote social progress, better standards of life and greater freedom. This is the fundamental commitment that the international community has made: These are the values that Canada defends and will continue to defend with conviction.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise in this House today to draw attention to International Human Rights Day. Today we celebrate the 43rd anniversary of the world's adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
December 10, 1991

I agree with the minister. The world has changed radically since December 10, 1948. Some progress has been made in the world political scene. The Soviet Union, as an example, no longer exists as we knew it. This former superpower is now more than willing to work with its former adversary, the United States, to seek common ground on global issues rather than pursue the previous path of a balance of terror.
The Berlin Wall has come down, highlighting the end of the cold war and revolutionary changes throughout eastern Europe. Several African, Asian and American countries are choosing democracy. There is a world-wide movement toward democracy and no longer will people quietly be subject to authoritarian rule.
1991 has become the year in which we have become evermore aware of the tragic victims of violence around the world. Since we last proclaimed International Human Rights Day, the world has been at war with Iraq.
Yugoslavia continues to tear itself apart amidst ongoing violent struggle. In the Middle East, though human rights violations continue there is a beacon of hope with the peace talks.
A new internationalism is waiting to be bom, based on the common goals of the elimination of poverty, a recognition of the fragility of the environment, and the slow recognition of the basic rights and dignity of every person and people.
Everywhere, including former Soviet socialist republics, the struggle for self-determination is the order of the day. The key word here is the word "struggle". With the freedom we enjoy as Canadians comes a responsibility to help reshape and redefine a new world order.
Canada has had a tradition of pursuing an international foreign policy, particularly under Prime Ministers St. Laurent, Pearson and Trudeau. As we face new challenges we can again be a voice in this birth of international co-operation, openness and compassion which will seek to free all people.
My leader, the leader of the Liberal Party, said in a foreign policy speech over a year ago:
I am realistic about our ability to influence the course of events in
a world where others often have larger stakes, or larger means, than
Routine Proceedings
ours. But Canada does have a respected voice and shares legitimate interests with many countries. We lead when we contribute a well-rounded vision of the world, or when we speak up for international law and mediation, or when we show that we care for those who suffer elsewhere in the world.
The minister speaks of Canada's support for international institutions such as the United Nations or the government's stated policies in favour of human rights and democratic development in our bilateral relations. Of late, however, there have been many examples in which the actions have not lived up to the rhetoric.
I think particularly of East Timor. It was not until yesterday that the government suspended approval of new aid projects to Indonesia as a sign of indignation following the recent massacre by Indonesian troops of an estimated 200 unarmed East Timorese.
This tiny nation was struggling toward independence and self-determination only to be invaded by Indonesia in 1975. The people of East Timor have suffered one of the most ruthless attacks in modem history. On a per capita basis the atrocities committed against the small population of less than a million people are higher than those committed by, as an example, the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia. As many as one-third of the people of this small south Pacific island have perished due to the initial war and subsequent acts of violence, starvation and disease perpetrated by the Indonesian army.
This week December 7, 1991 was the 16th anniversary of this invasion and the action of this government. While we recognize it, I am afraid it could be too little too late.
Indonesia, by its invasion and occupation of East Timor, has embarked on gross violations of the United Nations two most basic principles of integrity of territory and the right to self-determination. The United Nations Security Council has passed resolutions calling for the withdrawal of Indonesia, yet Canada is one of only two hold-out nations. The government has recognized Indonesia's de facto rule over East Timor. Canada has at the UN voted against resolutions calling for Indonesia's withdrawal. We should all be ashamed of that.
In order for Canada to be legitimate in its condemnation of Indonesia's abhorrent actions against East Timor, it must immediately and unequivocally offer support for

December 10, 1991
Routine Proceedings
all UN resolutions regarding Indonesia's illegal occupation of East Timor.
We must press for implementation of the UN Security Council's resolutions 389 and 384, which call for the immediate withdrawal of Indonesian troops and for international assistance to the people of East Timor.
A quotation of Mr. Andrei Sakharov, Oxford, 1986, comes to mind: "Human rights will not be helped by silence". In silence we are as guilty as the perpetrator of the human rights violations. This government has been selectively silent. The Prime Minister has made lofty pronouncements of a policy that would see the linkage of Canadian aid to a country's human rights record. We have yet to learn how the policy will work. There appears to be a double standard in its implementation. For example, why has the policy of this government been to treat the invasion of Kuwait differently than the invasion of East Timor?
I recommend developing and defining the criteria for implementing this stated policy with the following in mind: transparency, consistency, coherency and compassion.
In closing I would like to honour this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, Aung San Suu Kyi, for her non-violent struggle to restore democratic freedom to her country of Myanmar, formerly Burma. She has paid a dear price for exemplifying the values that we are commemorating on this day of international human rights.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to join in commemorating today the 43rd anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It is an opportunity for us to review the progress that has been made toward equality and fundamental respect for human rights but also to underline the many challenges that face us still today in the world on this front and at home in Canada.
Internationally I would remind the House that the Universal Declaration of Human Rights encompasses civil and political rights as well as the economic, social and cultural rights. These aspects of human rights are profoundly important. Frank Scott, the distinguished Canadian poet, author, lawyer and constitutional human
rights expert, said: "The trappings of democracy hang loosely on an emaciated body politic".
We know this only too well in a world in which 40,000 children die each day from preventable disease and from hunger. We know this from reading the annual reports of UNICEF on the state of the world's children. We know there are over one million poor children in Canada. It is a national disgrace. At the same time globally the world spends over $900 billion on weapons of destruction.
Surely it is time to recognize that the real threats to security globally are poverty, hunger, homelessness, sickness, AIDS and the global destruction of our environment.
The Prime Minister has spoken of the importance of the linkage between human rights and Canada's aid policies and hopefully our trade policies as well. We in this House support that, but there remains a huge gap between the rhetoric and the reality.
For example, we heard just last night in the external affairs committee from representatives of NGOs who are working courageously and diligently on the issue of self-determination for the people of East Timor.
We also heard from government representatives who suggested that they are not prepared to impose an arms embargo on Indonesia and are not prepared to support self-determination resolutions at the United Nations. This suggests that they are not prepared to encourage actively an international independent inquiry into the murders at Dili on November 12.

When we talk about basic rights, we must not forget that economic, social, civil and political rights as recognized internationally are linked, especially when we are talking about developing countries.
Canada must not pressure countries receiving assistance into adopting economic policies designed by international financial institutions which ignore the economic and social rights of the poor. Canada must maintain the same standards for international financial institutions.

Amnesty International has documented many other areas in which there are profound abuses of human rights: Burma, today we pay tribute to the recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize Aung San Suu Kyi; China, including Tibet; Central America where over 70,000 people have died in the tragic war in El Salvador; Sri Lanka; India, particularly in the Kashmir and in the Punjab; Mexico; South Africa where apartheid is not dead; Togo where the fragile new democracy has been
December 10, 1991

overturned by a military invasion; and the Middle East where human rights continue to be violated whether it is the rights of 4,500 Syrian Jews who continue to be denied the most fundamental rights or whether it is the rights of the Palestinians who yesterday commemorated the fourth anniversary of the intifada. Certainly the time for justice for the Palestinians, for self-determination, for recognition of their right to nationhood and for an end to human rights violations has come. Indeed it should have come long ago.
We have seen violations in Croatia, in Vojvodina and in Kosovo. There has been a tragic loss of life and the destruction of the cultural heritage of a people.

We extend a warm welcome to Jean-Bertrand Aristide who is here in Ottawa, and we wish him a speedy return to Haiti as the president of that country.

In closing, I would remind the House that Canada must also practise at home what we preach abroad with respect to human rights. In that light the inter-church committee for refugees has reminded us of the importance that Canada not remain silent to abuses of refugees and asylum seekers in developed countries. Canada should do far more to respond to documented human rights problems with our own refugee programs in Canada.
Finally I would remind the House that the Canadian Human Rights Act must be amended. We have waited far too long for equality, equality for lesbians and gay men who were promised that equality five and a half years ago. They are still denied equality. We need equality for people with disabilities, for people of colour who still feel the sting of racism, for women who are still second-class citizens in Canada and for aboriginal peoples. The treatment of them at home remains a national shame and a national tragedy.
Both internationally and here at home much work remains to be done. Many challenges remain. We celebrate the accomplishments that have been made today on International Human Rights Day. We pay tribute to individuals who are working in NGOs both in Canada and internationally. We must remember much work
Routine Proceedings
remains to be done to realize the principle that was set out so eloquently.

Jean-Bertrand Aristide last night in Montreal told us: "Human rights are the torch that lights modem democracy".
That is true, so let us make sure it is true in Canada and throughout the world.
I believe it would be appropriate to remind the House of the order of business at this point. We are now on Presenting Reports from Interparliamentary Delegations, under Routine Proceedings.

subsubtopic: CONGRATULATIONS TO AUNG SAN SUU KYI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have consulted with my colleagues on all sides of the House and I believe that there would be agreement to the following motion:
That this House express its congratulations to Aung San Suu Kyi, recipient of 1991 Nobel Peace Prize being presented in Oslo today, for her courage, integrity and commitment to the Burmese people's struggle for human rights and democracy.
It calls upon the state law and order restoration council of Burma to honour the results of the 1990 national election, to free Aung San Suu Kyi and the 62 jailed members of Parliament, and to allow her to give her speech of acceptance at this highest of awards from her home in Rangoon.
I believe this would meet with the agreement of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate our caucus with this resolution, especially on a day when humankind's highest award is given to the Leader of the Opposition in Burma.

I think this Parliament must go on record as supporting this resolution in particular in the hope that we can urge our own government to add its voice continually for the freedom of Aung San Suu Kyi. It is absolutely essential that her voice be added to the peaceful voices in this world.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to present a number of petitions signed by people from Windsor, Ontario and various centres in Ontario.
The petitions bear close to 8,000 names. They call upon Parliament to pass legislation establishing mandatory minimum sentences for all violent crimes which would apply uniformly to all regions of Canada.

subsubtopic: HATZIC ROCK SITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to present a petition signed predominantly by people from the riding of Mission-Coquitlam.
They are petitioning the government to recognize the Hatzic rock site near Mission, B.C. to be of great historical and spiritual value to the Sto:Lo people and to the people of Mission-Coquitlam.
We therefore ask the government to proceed with the necessary steps to see that the site is preserved and protected as a national heritage site.

subsubtopic: UKRAINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by residents of my constituency of Burnaby-Kingsway, as well as residents of other parts of British Columbia and Quebec.
They point out that on August 24, 1991 the Ukrainian Parliament declared Ukrainian independence and the creation of an independent and democratic state of Ukraine. One million Canadians of Ukrainian descent have for a century sustained their ideals of freedom and democracy for an independent ancestral homeland.
They go on to point out some of the other history leading to the historic referendum just recently in Ukraine. Finally they call upon the Parliament of Canada to urge the government to give genuine support to the people of Ukraine by officially recognizing Ukraine's independence and establishing full diplomatic relations with the government and people of Ukraine immediately following the positive referendum on December 1 of this year.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Question No. 145 will be answered today.

1.	Since 1984, with respect to applications for (a) War Veterans Widows Allowance, (b) GIS, (c) Survivor Disability Pension, (i) how many late claims have been received (ii) how many late claims have been accepted?
2.	What has been the estimated savings to the government in non-payment of these benefits to eligible persons?

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Governement in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Veterans Affairs and National Health and Welfare as follows:
1.	(a) With respect to retroactivity for war veterans allowance, there is no provision in the War Veterans Allowance Act to authorize payments for any period prior to the first day of the month in which the application was made. This is a matter of legislation and there is no discretionary power to alter it. With respect to the hon. member's question, then, there are no "late claims" for war veterans allowance purposes.
(c) There is no deadline for applying for survivor benefits under the Pension Act. When benefits are awarded to a survivor of a disability pensioner, the effective date of the award is the later of either the day following the death of the disability pensioner or three years prior to the date of the decision to award survivor benefits.
2.	Because there is no provision within the WVA Act to authorize payments for any period prior to the first day of the month of application the question with regard to estimated savings is not relevant.
It is not possible to determine, or to estimate with any degree of accuracy, the number of applications for survivor benefits which may have been affected by the retroactivity limits of the Pension Act.

1. (b) and 2. At the present time, the Old Age Security benefit system does not maintain payment history on each beneficiary. Therefore, extensive research involving administrative costs and person-year utilization would be required to capture the requested information.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition) moved
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
That this House condemn the government for economic
mismanagement that has led to an intolerable and tragic level of
unemployment, business failure and poverty in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House today, December 10, especially since exactly one year ago the constituents of Beausejour did me the honour of electing me as their member. I wish to thank them for doing so.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
I had the honour and the privilege to be elected in a riding that truly represents what is best in this country, where the two-thirds of the population that is French speaking lives on friendly terms with the other one-third that is English speaking, in southeastern New Brunswick. This people are hard workers and as Canadians they are very proud of their linguistic and cultural diversity. The two-thirds who are French speaking are descendants of those people who were deported and then came back, and they truly believe in the French language and culture and are very proud to be Canadians and to be part of Canadian society.

In every day of their lives we see examples of what is possible in Canada. The francophone Acadians who make up two-thirds of Beausejour are working side by side with anglophones who make up one-third and have strong roots in Canada. Many of them were Loyalists who came from the United States to live under the Canadian regime. They have shown to this country that it is possible to live and work together in harmony. It has been a great experience and a great honour for me to be the member for Beausejour for the last 12 months.
I would like to congratulate my colleague from York North who is celebrating his comeback to the House. He is one of the few in this House who has had the occasion to sit twice in one Parliament. All of us are very proud to have him as a colleague and we want to extend our congratulations for his second election in one term.

I am moving this motion as a condemnation of this government's economic policies. Of course, at the end of the year, in the festive season, we would like to be able to get up with a smile on our lips and say that we face the new year with great optimism.

We have to recognize that the government's mishandling of the economy has caused the worst and longest economic crisis since the 1930s. Every family, every community, every region of the country and every sector of the economy are being hurt.
For the last three years we have been saying to this government that the mix of economic policies it was developing was the wrong one. Yet it is still on it.
For the last three years the one obsession of this government has been to fight inflation at any cost. What has been the result of this policy that led to a high dollar and high interest rates? What is the situation today in Canada?
Somebody said this terrible economic strategy of the government is more or less a political version of the neutron bomb. The buildings are left standing but inside all the people have been destroyed.
We have 1.5 million Canadians today who are not working. In less than a year in Canada we have had
60,000	bankruptcies, either personal or business. We can talk about anything we want in this economy today and it is a disaster. Look at what happened in our cities. In the city of Toronto and the city of Montreal what do we see? It is a complete disaster. In fact in any big city in Canada we find that the fastest growing sector of the economy is food banks and soup kitchens.
In Toronto there are more than 100,000 people on welfare. Some 120,000 people have to go to food banks and one-third of these people are children.
December 10, 1991



Today the fair city of Montreal, which a few years ago said that it had pride, has unemployment. Thirty per cent of the citizens of greater Montreal receive unemployment insurance or welfare or some form of government assistance, and that is a disaster.
If you go to Montreal or other parts of Quebec, as I have, you see that people are completely demoralized. The same thing goes throughout the country. People are leaving the rural areas of Quebec to go to live in Montreal, but of course they do not find work. Nothing is more depressing today than walking down Ste. Catherine Street in Montreal. You see one closed store after another. That is the result of this government's economic policies.
We could talk about many other sectors like agriculture, for example. If any industry was stable even in Ontario it was agriculture, because in the past 10 years, marketing boards had stabilized it and balanced production with demand so that consumers had fixed, predictable prices and farmers had stable incomes.
But what is happening today? Because of this government's poor strategy, we are wondering what will happen with GATT. No one knows. If article XI were abolished, what would happen to marketing boards? What did the government do in the Free Trade Agreement? It completely gave up the possibility of setting up bilateral tariff barriers with the American market in case the GATT decision was unfavorable to farmers. Over the past 10 or 12 years, we had managed to stabilize that sector with some effort. It is now very uncertain and thousands of jobs are at stake.

I could talk about western farmers, not only those who need supply management in Canada. Wheat is at its lowest price since the depression. Farmers are leaving their farms every day, to go where? There is no place to go. If they go to the city there are no jobs. There are families who are losing their life assets day after day after day, and they really do not know what will happen to them. It is almost unbelievable.
In Beausejour, Manitoba they have established a food bank for farmers. These are the very people whose job is to create food for our table and who do not have enough
Supply
for themselves. We have never seen such a disaster in Canada. When does the government give some help? It just does that under a lot of pressure in the middle of an election, cynically to show that it can buy votes. Wait until the next election. It will not be able to buy one vote. I can guarantee that.
What about the fisheries and overfishing? There is no control over foreign ships that come and take over Canadian resources. We protect the fish on the Grand Banks, for example, off the coast of Newfoundland with conservation measures. We restrain our own fishermen from taking too much fish.
What happens? At the other end of the banks the foreign companies come and pick up the fish. There is no passport for fish. They do not know if they are in Canadian or international waters. Neither the international community nor this government is putting pressure on these countries that are abusing the situation. They are depleting resources that have been there for centuries.

I was in my riding of Beausejour on the weekend and I met fishermen and people who work in the processing plants in Cap-Pele. Cap-Pele has perhaps the largest concentration of this kind of smokehouse in America, if not the world. These people worked very hard all year. Companies have built up considerable inventories. And what happens? Suddenly, but quite properly, the government embargoes products sent to Haiti, the main customer. But who pays? The fishermen and entrepreneurs, who are all small business people, and the government does nothing. We have called CIDA but have not heard back. We should not destroy this industry. I am not saying that there should not be economic sanctions against Haiti, but on the other hand this kind of food keeps and the government should do something. This was directly caused by a government policy, although well intentioned and one that looks good around the world. But the government does not pay the cost of it. Who pays? The fishermen and smokehouse operators in Cap-Pele, New Brunswick, in the riding of Beausejour. I hope that someone at CIDA is listening to us and will realize that they are working against a traditional industry that has been profitable for many years, that they are ruining it, perhaps even destroying it forever.

December 10, 1991
Supply
That is the kind of policy this government implements all the time. I could talk about plant closures.
Industries are closing down all over Canada. When we had the recession 10 years ago in 1982 they were closing down for a period of time. Now they are closing down forever. They are moving to the United States because of the free trade agreement. This government does not want to do anything.
I could talk about the trade deficit. For the first time in 15 years we have a merchandise trade deficit in Canada. We used to have a balance of payments problem but not a merchandise trade deficit. It is like that all over Canada, and this government is doing nothing at all. Why? It is because the government stubbornly has a fix on inflation and this is destroying everything.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance was in Montreal. He had discussions with business people and they said they wanted a lower Canadian dollar and they wanted to be competitive.
I remember what was said by the manufacturing sector in Canada at the time of the free trade agreement. They said: "Okay, we can sign that, but we need a dollar that will remain competitive". But this government has refused to recognize that reality because some government advisers have the gall to say that we will endure 30 per cent unemployment if we can have zero inflation. They should know that 30 per cent unemployment is a revolution. When you administer the economic and monetary policies of this country, you cannot have a fix only on inflation. You have to have a fix on employment and competition too. That it is exactly what we said to this government.
During the fall I travelled this country and talked about the five principles that we need to restore Canada. We said one of the first things we need is to restore Canada's industrial strength. The only instrument available to them in the very difficult world we are living in today is a competitive dollar. It is always a high dollar. Why? We do not know why. Is it because there are those who say we should have zero inflation that they are afraid to attain anyway?
Mr. James Baker, when he was the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, said: "We have no trade problem with Canada. The only problem we are having with Canada is the level of the Canadian dollar". Since the government signed the free trade agreement the dollar has been kept high. You have to look at all the reasons. The minister will get up and say that the interest rates are going down. They are going down, but today the government rate is still three points above that of the United States. Of course the prime rate has been reduced, but the government rate is 3.04 per cent above. Yes, sir. I checked this morning. You can say whatever you want, but it is-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: You are right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
It is 3.04. Why is this? Because this government has a deliberate policy to make sure that the Canadian dollar remains high. It is why the investor is looking to buy Canadian dollars. The prime rate has gone down, but the main rate has not gone down. There is still a spread of three points. So let us get the dollar lower.
The minister will tell us that he cannot lower the dollar. I have been Minister of Finance. I know that the government intervenes strongly or less strongly. I was there. At that time it was at 93 cents, but because we wanted to make sure that the industry in the riding of the minister in British Columbia could sell wood in the United States, we let the Canadian dollar go from 93 cents to 85 cents. We have to do that to the dollar, to make sure that we train our labour force, that we have research and development and that we have market support.
I could go on and on but apparently time is running short.

speechtext: More, more.

We have to reduce the tax burden of the middle class. This government has increased the taxes 32 times in the last few years. The gap between Canada and the United States in terms of the GDP and taxes is higher than ever before.
We have to make sure that we face competition today and with globalization that we have comprehensive and creative adjustment policies to make sure that those affected are not left in the cold like it is with this government. Nobody will do anything.
December 10, 1991

We have to make sure, as a fourth point, to balance regional economic growth because we cannot let only the market forces decide. There is nothing Canadian left on the shelves any more. This government has destroyed everything in terms of transportation and anything that was keeping this country together. What happens if we do not have any transportation? The people in Atlantic Canada are trapped there and remain poor.
We need a government that can intervene. It is why Japan and Germany are successful. The government intervenes there when it is needed. It is not a laissez-faire government like this one.
The fifth point of course is that they were elected to reduce the debt. Do you remember that, Mr. Speaker? When they started they said: "The $175 billion that these Liberals have left us is terrible". They worked on a program to reduce the debt. They worked very hard on it, and now the debt has been reduced to $400 billion. What a success, what a success.
I would like to say to everyone at the end of my remarks that people feel terrible in Canada but there is hope at the end of the tunnel. If this government has any decency within 12 months there will be an election. There was an election three years and one month ago so we should have an election in 1992.
I say to Canadians when I am travelling that we need a new government, but this new government will need a mission. This mission is to bring hope and pride to this nation as this government has failed to do. On every score this country is desperate today.
They have created a constitutional mess that we will try on a non-partisan basis to cure. If they had known better they would have shut up in 1987 when they were preoccupied in Quebec about having a new class of business people doing well in the world. They opened a wound that they will have a hell of a problem closing. We will help them.
I hope they will stop that nonsense of having a Spicer II show and doing what they are doing today. The NDP and ourselves put our feet on the ground and said: "We do not want that kind of show any more. We want the members to look at the 28 propositions". We went far to achieve that, but we have succeeded. I hope that we will be able to find a solution and bring hope. It is a problem
Supply
that need not have existed, but it was created by this government. The economic mess is there, as we all know, but we say to Canadians that there will be an election. There will be a government that will understand that we have no ambition in life to be the lap dog of the American presidency and that we can speak as proud Canadians. We will tell the people that we will have a government that cares for people.
We had the Aylmer conference where we had experts coming from all over the world who told us: "Yes, it is possible to take the challenge of globalization but maintain at the same time the social safety net that is the pride of Canada. If you have proud and independent people, you will not have people in misery. They will be able to compete in the world".
The government that we will be forming, if the election comes next year, if this government has the courage to consult the people, will be a government that will maintain the dignity of Canadians while at the same time preparing Canadians, training them, educating them and challenging them to be the most competent, the best educated people in North America.
We can be on top of the world if we have a government that cares for people, that restores pride in Canadians. We will go into the 21st century, as we should do, as a proud, independent Canada which will not be afraid of the globalization in the world, but will remain, as I like to say, a united country in its diversity that will be the envy of the world.

December 10, 1991

With the trade deal we have seen the loss of manufacturing jobs. Just last week Norsk Enterprises in Quebec said that the trade deal had caused it to lose its business and that it had to lay off more workers. That is the story right across Canada.
We gave away our access to oil and gas. We created a situation where social programs are being undermined through the trade deal. only responsible way to do it. We will get rid of the GST but we will have to find a clear alternative because we will be responsible. We will not be like the NDP.

Trust is the central issue in public life today. Canadians are saying from coast to coast to coast that they do not trust their politicians. What assurances can he give the people of Canada that the Liberal Party of Canada will have a value system that people can trust?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that it is a veiy good question. It is a very important problem in Canada today.

We say to the people that we will not buy their votes. We will be truthful to them. We will have an honest government. It will not be a government riddled with scandal like the one we have now. What is also important about the speech of the Leader of the Opposition is that it clearly accentuated and punctuated the differences that exist between the political parties in Canada and the clear and the precise economic agenda that the Liberal Party has proposed to Canadians.
December 10, 1991

My question to the Leader of the Opposition concerns the high unemployment rate among young people. In this country 400,000 young people in total are unemployed. I would like to ask the Leader of the Opposition to comment on this extremely important national issue.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say I am enjoying very much the family feud that is going on. It is very enlightening. We have all garnered a certain amount of information about the formulation of policy and how it actually is formulated, sort of on the run and in the House of Commons.
The hon. member and the member for Broadview- Greenwood talk about trust. The Leader of the Opposition says: "We will scrap the GST and, trust me, I will bring in an alternative".
Well, he is going to have to get a little more specific than that. Oh, I am sure he will. Him and Preston Manning will certainly be able to give us a lot of enlightenment on that one.
Yes, it is the Christmas spirit. Yes, it is. I thought for starters that one would want to look at the record of a government of which the hon. Leader of the Opposition was a member. I just took a quick survey and 10 years ago today interest rates for an ordinary businessmen were running at about 18 to 20 per cent. He talks about spreads. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, the spread between the Canadian prime rate and the United States prime

December 10,1991
Supply
rate is about half of 1 per cent. The Canadian prime rate, the lowest in 18 years, is at 8 per cent. The American prime rate is at 7.5 per cent and if you want to go to three-month commercial paper, that spread is about 2.6 per cent. It hovers between 2.4 per cent and 2.6 per cent.
I think that factually the hon. Leader of the Opposition was wrong.
Let us look at the unemployment rate. It was running at about 11.2 per cent. The inflation rate was at 12.6 per cent, and what happened in the third quarter of 1981? The GDP fell by 3.5 percentage points. There you have a situation where this member is condemning the federal government for its economic mismanagement and all we saw during the time that he was a member of that government of which I spoke. We had our fill of fiscal irresponsibility and structural suffocation. That fiscal irresponsibility is placing a heavy burden, an undue burden, on all Canadians in terms of our ability to cope with a burden of debt and the cost of servicing that debt which is costing Canadians 35 cents for every taxpayer's dollar that they provide to the Government of Canada.
Let us review a little more of the record of the Leader of the Opposition while I have his attention. He condemns this government for fiscal mismanagement. When he served as President of the Treasury Board between 1974 and 1976, in two short years he spent-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: You're shameless, absolutely shameless.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if you want to give the hon. member a chance to speak I am sure that we can organize that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: The hon. member may very well seek time to speak but the hon. Minister of Finance has the floor and I know members would want to extend the courtesy of hearing him.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in two short years, between 1974 and 1976, he presided over a spending increase of 33 per cent and then he said at 16 per cent, when he increased the spending for one year, that that reflected great restraint.
In Mr. Macdonell's Auditor General's report in 1974-75, he said this, and I quote:
The present state of financial management and control systems of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada is significantly below acceptable standard of quality and effectiveness.
In September 1976 he wrote, and I quote:
I am deeply concerned that Parliament and indeed the government has lost or is close to losing effective control of the public purse.
That is the background around which we have to restore the fiscal integrity of this country and restore management. Again, giving an example of his managerial prowess, in a strike where public servants shut down the grain transportation sector for 31 days, he settled for a 29.25 per cent increase and he called that leadership.
Let us talk about the deficit when he was Minister of Finance. In 1977, the deficit the previous year had been $6.3 billion. The spring budget he brought in was to be a $7.2 billion deficit for 1977-78 and it ended up being a $10 billion deficit, a 70 per cent increase.
His next budget was a 30 per cent increase above the earlier one. That is where we got into this treadmill of spending. You know, spend today and borrow for tomorrow and place the burden on future generations.
He talks about the control he had over the Bank of Canada and how he manipulated the exchange rate. Well, here are some quotes out of Hansard that clearly demonstrate the opposite of his allegation that he had just presented to the House of Commons. He said on February 27, 1978, in a speech to The Canadian Club in Montreal, and I quote:
Market forces should continue to determine the appropriate exchange value for our currency.
Another quote in Hansard at page 1222, November 17, 1978. He said, and I quote:
We do not intend to fix the rate of the Canadian dollar. The rate will be fixed by the market.
And then another quote, in which he said the following:
Our monetary policy is set by the Governor of the Bank of Canada and I do not intend to ask him to change his policy.
That quotation is from Hansard page 1635, December 7, 1977.
December 10, 1991

What the hon. member is saying here today is all hogwash. He talks a good line. He said something when he was sitting over here on the treasury benches. He had one position. Now that he is over there on the opposition benches he clearly has another position. That has to be taken into consideration as we focus on this particular debate.
There is no question, and no one can argue with the fact that the economy is emerging from a very difficult period. It has been a painful period for many Canadians. Coming out of a recession and through a period of transition where we see the need for a structural adjustment and change has placed very severe difficulties upon all segments of the Canadian economy.
I indicated in my appearance before the House committee last month that the recession had been a little deeper than expected and that the pace of recovery had been somewhat slower than we had anticipated. However, one has to view this in the changing circumstances that have occurred throughout the world. The world economy, for example, as I have indicated on many occasions, grew by some 2 per cent in 1990. It will grow by a meagre 1 per cent in 1991 and it is expected to grow something around 3 per cent or less in 1992. As a matter of fact, I have before me a headline from The Ottawa Citizen which says that the world economy is at its worst since 1945.
The growth rate of 1 per cent in 1991 has been the worst since 1981 or 1982. One has to look at the Canadian situation in that context and I have to remind hon. members that all industrialized nations have been revising their growth projections downward. I also have to advise hon. members that the only two countries that will experience an improvement in the unemployment situation in 1992, according to the Conference Board of Canada, are the United States and Canada. All other industrialized countries, particularly those in the G-7, will experience an increase in unemployment during
1992.	I say that because we are going through difficult times and Canada is affected by it because we are a global trader, a world player. We cannot deny that.
There are some positive things that are occurring. I think they have to be recorded and that hon. members have to be reminded. Inflation has dropped significantly
Supply
to just 1.6 per cent on annualized basis over the last six months. That is the lowest in 20 years.
I talked about interest rates. The prime rate at 8 per cent is the lowest rate of interest in 18 years. That is a remarkable achievement. There are other positive indicators on the horizon that came out in the third quarter annual accounts.
The corporate profits are strengthening. You need corporate profits if you are going to have investment in plant and equipment. They increased by 15 per cent on an annualized basis. The latest data indicate that personal income rose by 4.4 per cent over last year and personal disposable income by 4.6 per cent.
What is also interesting is that the savings rate of Canadians has increased from an average of 9 to 9.5 per cent to about 11 per cent. I have to remind hon. members that every one percentage point increase in the national savings, personal savings, reduces consumption by about $4.5 billion. Put another way, if that saving rate had not increased from 9 per cent to 11 per cent there would be an additional $9 billion out there for goods and services consumption.
It is quite obvious that Canadians are saving more because there is uncertainty and because there is lack of confidence in the economy. That is true, but some day soon that money will be spent.
The goods producing sector is another very important indicator in the third quarter statistics. The goods producing sector increased by 5.2 per cent. The other thing that should be noted is that in a survey by the 300 large corporations that are operating in Canada they had indicated that they would increase their capital spending by some 5.2 per cent in 1992. That too is good news.
Mortgage rates have come down dramatically and a person renewing a $75,000 mortgage will see a saving of something between $275 and $300 per month on his monthly mortgage payments. That is a major decline. That puts additional income in the pockets of Canadians for spending on consumer goods and services.
Housing starts are another important indicator which should bring us some comfort. The increase in the residential investment sector was some 17.2 per cent in the third quarter. Housing starts have been increasing to the level of roughly 200,000 on an annualized basis. The

December 10,1991
Supply
data coming out are not uniform. The data are erratic, and that is not unusual coming out of a recession.
We said in the budget of 1991 that growth would re-emerge in the second half of 1991. Colleagues certainly did not condemn the government for being overly conservative in that projection, but the fact of the matter is that growth re-emerged in the second quarter. It was originally quoted at 4.9 per cent real and in the third quarter accounts that was adjusted upward to 5.7 per cent. That is a remarkable turnaround when you consider that there was a decline of 4.9 per cent in the fourth quarter of 1990 and a decline of 4.7 per cent in the first quarter of 1991. To have a turnaround of 5.7 per cent positive in the second quarter was a dramatic turnaround.
Obviously no one expected that kind of recoveiy to be sustainable. We did have a lower rate of growth in the third quarter, .9 per cent, but when you average the two you end up with an average rate of growth over a six-month period of 3.3 per cent. I think that is not bad considering the depth of this recession, much deeper than we expected. We expected a peak decline of about
2.5	per cent. It declined closer to 2.8 per cent. The fact of the matter is that the recession accompanied by the need to readjust and to restructure is making this issue much more complicated and much more critical.
I should remind the House that in the early stages of the recovery, going back to 1981 and 1982, we had the similar kind of data coming out that were quite variable. As a matter of fact, in the ninth and the twelfth months of recovery in 1983-84 period we actually had negative growth.
I am just going through some of the quotes of expert analysts and journalists. In the 1982-83 newspapers there are articles on months one to three of the recoveiy. In a The Globe and Mail article by columnist Peter Cook there is a headline "Deteriorating Conditions Suggest a Renewal of Slump". On December 7 there was a headline "Economic News Bad to Worse".
On December 30, two months into the recoveiy, one read "Few Signs that Relief is Imminent". Again bad economic news predominates. You then get into four to six months of recovery. One headline is "Progress Uncertain in Real Economy. Upturn Begun but Still
Weak". On April 6 one headline read "The Rate of Recovery in Manufacturing Begins to Falter." On July 22, 1983 another read "Don't Depend on Consumers Alone".
On August 2, 1983, 10 to 12 months into recovery, the headline is posing the question "Is Economic Recovery Faltering?" We go again to August 31, 1983. The Globe and Mail headline was "Experts see Signs of Recovery Slowing". We go on to October 1. The Star Phoenix says that the economic news was glum.
We are going through that kind of a situation. The fact of the matter is that we are going to have these kinds of volatile data that will be coming out and that will require explanation.
The fact of the matter is that we still remain confident that growth in 1992 will be something in the range of 3 per cent to 3.5 per cent. The latest survey conducted by the finance department and the private sector forecasts the growth rate to be something in the order of 3.5 per cent.
The IMF's most recent forecast suggests a growth rate of 3.8 per cent. The OECD suggests a growth rate of 3.5 per cent. The Conference Board of Canada suggests a growth rate of something in excess of 4 per cent. By historical standards, this is a moderate to modest recovery.
The fact of the matter is that we must continue to maintain our policy stance of declining inflation and the maintenance of low interest because that will produce the growth and that will produce the long-term jobs.
Inflationary policies which are being advocated by members across will not produce the goods, will not produce the services, will not produce the jobs and will not produce the long-term prosperity for Canada, and history really proves that.
By historical standards we know that this recovery is slow because of our inability, and we do not have the luxury of injecting fiscal stimulus. The hon. member should understand that. We must deal with the issues that are really confronting us. The issues are not only coming out of the recession, but how we can be more competitive and how we can be more productive. In that connection, it requires the co-operation, co-ordination and leadership of all segments of society.
December 10, 1991

In The Globe and Mail, I believe on Saturday, I noticed what the chairman of Ford Motor Company had to say about Ontario's policies. I am not here to pick on Ontario. I only use this to demonstrate the necessity for co-ordinating economic policy in this country. The headline says that our entrepreneurs are afraid to invest in Ontario. Mr. Harrigan said:
Ontario's economic policies are placing roadblocks in the way of the recovery and scaring away investment.
Frankly entrepreneurs are afraid to invest in Ontario. The auto industry is apprehensive about labour changes that will make it easier to unionize, particularly auto parts companies. A strike at one of these companies would close down operations of the Canadian and U.S. car makers which rely on just in time parts delivery schedules. Eighty per cent of our production is exported to the United States.
I say that we must co-ordinate our policies in such a way that we can meet the challenges we face. Canada is a trading nation. We are the seventh largest trading nation in the world. We must trade to survive.
We must meet the challenge of globalization. We must meet the challenges of improving our productivity. The foundation of prosperity had been rotting away when we came into office. It required some major structural changes such as getting the deficit under control, making those structural changes such as deregulation, bringing about a free trade agreement and trade liberalization, scrapping FIRA, scrapping the National Energy Program and creating an investment climate in which Canadians would invest, in which the skill and the spirit of enterprises could flourish.
This is the kind of framework that we put in place. We have made the structural changes. We are getting the fiscal and monetary fundamentals correct. We have provided the foundation for strong sustainable growth with price stability. That will produce the growth. That will produce the jobs and that will produce security for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I address my comments and question to the minister, may I say that this is what Canadians expect from Parliament. This is the best of Parliament today and
Supply

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in the debate today.
It is important that we in this House are debating the economy and putting forth the kind of alternatives that we as parties propose. We did not hear many alternatives from the government or from the opposition, but what we can see in terms of what is happening to Canada today is that this government's economic policies have failed.
Indeed the neo-Conservative economic policies of both this government and former Liberal governments have led us to where we are today.
I do not believe I need to go on in any great length about the record of this government. Virtually every day in Question Period we raise questions with the government asking whether it will be open to changing the economic policies which are destroying this country. Every day we get the same answers. It is closed to listening to what Canadians have to say and it is certainly closed to the alternatives that this party has put forward. What this government cannot ignore is the 1.5 million unemployed in this country. This government cannot
December 10, 1991

ignore the other 1.5 million who are on social assistance or unemployment insurance.
The record small business bankruptcies, the record number of farm bankruptcies and the industrial sector in this country that is rapidly disappearing are all characteristics of our economy and are directly related to the policies of this government. Millions of Canadians are living in poverty. One in six children is living in poverty. An increase in food banks and an increase in the number of homeless necessitate action now. The homeless, the poor, the unemployed and those on assistance cannot wait until the middle of 1992 or 1993. They need help now.
When this government was first elected in 1984 no one, not even its strongest opponents, could have imagined the depth to which it would take the Canadian economy. No one could imagine the extent to which this government, which called social programs a sacred trust, would diminish social programs in this country. No one could have imagined a country that had so much to look forward to now has so much to regret.
This government was elected, I might say with some enthusiasm, in 1984. It was returned with reluctance in 1988 and in the next election this government will be turfed out where it belongs for the destruction it has done to Canada.

What Canadians have learned in the last decade is that neo-Conservative policies do not work. They do not work with a Liberal government and they do not work with a Conservative government. I am talking about high interest rates, an overvalued Canadian dollar, the trade agreement between Canada and the United States, the GST, privatization and deregulation.
Let us be concise and to the point. Each one of these policies has been a total disaster. All together, they have meant economic ruin for Canadian families. The GST is perhaps the best example of these destructive economic policies. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has explained how this sales tax is destroying our country's small businesses. It has reduced the purchasing power of consumers, undermined consumer confidence and encouraged Canadians to shop in the U.S.

My caucus, my party and I remain firm. This deal has cost hundreds of thousands of Canadians their jobs. It has undermined social programs in this country. It has meant that we cannot even use our own oil and gas resources in a way that is favourable to our economy. The deal must go and must be abrogated.

Mr. Speaker, the comments I have to make in the next while are very much comments on paradise lost and a bit of despair that we are ever going to see paradise regained.
I want to talk about the code words of the years since 1984. I want to talk about the code words that have become empty words, hollow words, unkept promises and failed dreams for Canadians. I want to start with the most famous of the empty words that we have heard from this government and this Prime Minister about jobs, jobs, jobs.
Unemployment in this country right now is affecting
1.5	million people. That means there is virtually nobody in this country whose family, friends, neighbours are not touched by the devastation of being without a job and
adequate income to provide for one's family, survival and comfort.
Unemployment has been accompanied by a dramatic increase in the number of bankruptcies and is partially the result of a dramatically increased number of bankruptcies. This government that came into office promising that Canada was open for business does not understand small business. It does not understand that 80 per cent of the new jobs in this country come from small independent Canadian owned businesses. Its policies have been devastating to those very businesses that are essential if we are to get Canadians working again.
On a larger scale, we have now lost .5 million manufacturing jobs. The number is bad enough but nearly one-quarter of the nation's manufacturing capacity is gone. It has gone in a very short period of time as a result of the policies of this government.
Getting Canada working means getting Canadians working again. Canadians working means people have income, are paying taxes and are able to buy goods and services that create jobs for other Canadians. It means a drop in the number of people who have to turn to government to help them through these difficult times with unemployment insurance and social services programs.
Jobs, jobs, jobs are empty words, hollow words for millions of Canadians today, and for more that 1.5 million over the course of this year. It is especially devastating when we know the extent to which it is affecting young children. This should be a happy time of year, but families are worried about their very survival and are unable to celebrate and join in sharing the joy of the season.
I want to talk about the other code words: globalization, competitiveness and free trade. Canadians know nothing is free and they are only discovering now how much free trade is costing us.
I remind the government that when it did its predictions on free trade and the benefits, not too many Canadians believed them. But the government believed, even it knew that any benefits to come from the free trade agreement were based on a dollar that was at maximum 85 cents.

December 10, 1991

For every one-hundredth of a penny the dollar went over 85 cents would in fact be negative effects of free trade. Yet it has consistently allowed the dollar to go and stay close to 90 cents.
The high interest rate policy of this government has devastated Canadian businesses and manufacturers. There have been 33 new taxes since this government has come into office. We now have a trade deficit for the first time in 15 years. There is a trade deficit in manufactured goods. No wonder we have lost so much of our manufacturing base.
Even more importantly we have this attitude that somehow straight raw market forces are what builds a country and what will let us get out there and compete and prosper in the global community.
That has been the philosophy of this government since 1984, and we are not prospering. We are not growing. We are not competing. Instead we see an attitude of freeing capital to move anywhere it wants in the world. The government is seeking out the cheapest labour and resources and is more concerned about helping those global dollars than helping their people.
We see that as the attitude of this government. We are seeing a new economic colonialism that is prepared to say that those who have least in any country in the world will have even less than they have now.
The third code word I keep hearing from this government which has no substance behind it is that people are our most valuable resource. If that were true then why have we seen a cut in unemployment and a cut in services to help people when they are going through difficult times created by this government's made-in-Ca-nada recession?
Why have we seen hundreds of millions cut from training? Why have we seen no worker adjustment programs? Why have we seen no move on a good national apprenticeship programs? Why have we seen the devastation of science and research in this country so that our bright young scientists have to go south of the border or elsewhere in the world to use the talents that we as Canadians have paid to develop in them? Why can a bright young man with a Ph.D. and years of aeronautical experience in Canada not find a job and contribute to the growth of Canada and to our future?

Why do we now see in Ontario, the richest province in this country, an increase in welfare payments of only 2 per cent when inflation is 4 per cent and more? It is bare subsistence living for tens of thousands of Ontario families.
We are told: "Do without social programs. Do without education. Do without medicare. Do without training. Do without many of our social programs so that we can build an economy and have those things in the future". We see the doing without, but we do not see much of the future.
I want to speak briefly about the fourth code word, sustainable development. We know that our economic prosperity depends on the preservation of our resources. There is no area of economic growth or prosperity that does not depend on natural resources.
Yet we have a government that produces a well developed proposal for an economic union, but totally ignores the fact that sustainable development means integrating our environmental planning with our economic planning.
We have a government that is negotiating a new free trade deal, an economic instrument if ever there was one. It is refusing to integrate environmental considerations with that economic agreement.
I want to close briefly by talking about an experience I had a couple of weeks ago when I spoke to a small group of immigrants. A gentleman from El Salvador who has been here for about five years said to me: "What we cannot understand is why you have a government that keeps destroying things instead of building things".
I said: "You know, you just turned on a light in my head because all of you in this room have been in Canada less than seven years. You have never known another government besides the Conservative government. Let me tell you about when we had governments in this country that created medicare, that created the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, that created pensions and indexation so that people could live decently, that created unemployment insurance, that created legislation that protected workers". We had that kind of government in Canada and we will have it again when a Liberal government is returned to office. There is no hope for any improvement with this government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to debate a very important motion presented by the Leader of the Opposition.
This government was first elected seven years ago on a promise that it would put the economy back on a solid footing and get the national debt under control. I think, if it were not so serious for the future of Canada, those promises would be laughable.
Seven years ago the Conservatives were full of ideas. They were going to give Canadians an unheard level of prosperity. They were going to make Canada competitive with new research and development commitments. They were going to cut the tax burden and create a climate favourable to business and business activity and hence economic growth. So much potential, so much disappointment.
As we survey the economic landscape seven years after, we see the wreckage created by the Conservative economic agenda. We see the industrial heartland of Canada slowly shutting down as plant after plant closes up and heads elsewhere.
We see Montreal, formerly a vibrant manufacturing centre, being turned into a desert where 11.8 per cent are unemployed. We see the farmers in the west and the fishermen in the east being told by the federal government that the cupboard is bare.
There is definitely anger in the land. The farmers, the fishermen and the unemployed are getting tired of this government's indifference and excuses. The government tries to pin the blame on past administrations but after seven years that excuse is wearing thin. After all, its blunders stand alone.
December 10, 1991

Supply
We can look at the national debt. In only seven years the Conservatives took the debt that had accumulated from 1867 to 1984 and nearly tripled it to over $400 billion. That is, I believe, an incontestable example of bad management.
The Conservatives also promised to get the deficit under control. Yet, even though they governed during the record boom years, they never managed to bring the deficit under $28 billion. The Tories can come up with all kinds of excuses, but the fact remains that these people who were elected because they were perceived as competent money managers could not get the deficit under control even in the boom years of the mid-1980s.
They could not get the deficit under control despite massive spending cuts and tax increases which have resulted in an additional income tax burden of $1,500 per Canadian family. Even the GST, which has done so much damage to business and consumer confidence, has not brought down this deficit.
There are many other examples of their economic mismanagement. In September Canada suffered its first trade deficit in 15 years. For a country like ours which is so dependent on trade, that is cause for alarm. Last month the Canadian economy lost another 49,000 jobs. This was added to 1.5 million Canadians who are unemployed, but it was not reflected in the unemployment rate because 45,000 Canadians left the labour force. In other words, things got so bad for them for so long that the people's UI is running out and they are giving up and joining the welfare rolls of this country.
Speaking of people giving up, what of the 250,000 manufacturing jobs which have vanished since 1988? In the 1988 election the Prime Minister told Canadians not to worry about free trade because there were going to be adjustment programs for displaced workers. Three years later those programs are only on paper.
Conservative mismanagement is easy to explain. They have no coherent plans. They have no master plan, no innovative plan to deal with the emerging global marketplace. The old ways of doing economics, raising taxes and cutting spending are no longer enough to deal with the new creative approaches used internationally.
I do not think that their strategy will make Canada globally competitive. It is no wonder that as a nation we are faring so badly. On the other hand, I must say that there is an answer and the Liberal Party of the 1990s has
a clear, precise and well planned agenda for rebuilding Canada's economy, an economy that since 1984 has been mismanaged to the point of causing unnecessary and irresponsible pain for Canadian small business, individuals, families and entire towns and cities.
We have a set of five Liberal principles on the economy. In restoring Canada's industrial strength, interest rates and the value of the Canadian dollar must be allowed to fall gradually, helping Canadians and their products to compete better internationally. New initiatives are required to promote labour force training, research and development and marketing support.
We must ensure a fair tax system. The Leader of the Opposition knows that the problems of unfair taxation cannot be solved overnight. While it would be responsible to offer tax cuts for everyone, Liberals have called for a fair tax system, especially to the middle class.
We have a comprehensive and creative adjustment policy. A Liberal government would introduce comprehensive adjustment programs to help both firms and workers adjust to the economic changes now in play.
Canada must help its workers to get the training they will need to have high skilled, high paying jobs in industries of the future. We must have balanced regional economic growth. All regions of Canada must be allowed to achieve their economic potential. Future industries should be based on the foundation of our existing resource industries and Canada should be seizing the opportunity in fast growing markets in Europe, Asia and the Pacific Rim.
We must have a fiscally responsible government. Canada's yearly deficits and accumulated debt are becoming an increasing drag on economic growth. The Leader of the Opposition has said that a Liberal government will scrutinize every line item of spending and only use government to do things it can and should do.
In conclusion, I would like to express the disappointment that all Canadians feel with this government's failed economic policies. Canadians, I truly believe, are not asking for too much. They want to feel that their government in Ottawa is fair, that their government is just, and that their government cares about their present state. Canadians want to feel that they live in a nation in which dreams and aspirations are still part of the national fibre. They want to know that their children

December 10, 1991

and their children's children live with the hope of a brighter tomorrow.
At a time when people need to be taken care of, the Conservative government is abdicating its responsibility to the citizens of this country. I hope the Leader of the Opposition's motion in this House today has rekindled some of the necessary human feelings, necessary human passions, that all governments must possess in order to bring back faith, confidence and trust in a nation that is presently searching for a sense of identity.
It is one year since I was re-elected to the House of Commons. I was really hoping that I could get up in this Chamber and bring good news to the residents of York North. Unfortunately today I have to rise once again and say that the conditions for the residents of York North and Canadians from coast to coast to coast are worse. There is a lack of confidence. There is a crisis in confidence in this country. I think the government must seriously look within itself and find the inner strength necessary to bring about the type of positive changes that will take care of Canadians, particularly those people who are being hit by this unfair and unjust economic recession that has created so much heartache in many families and in many communities.
