Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this debate today on the government's record in managing our economic affairs.
Unlike some of the other speakers who have spoken previously and who undoubtedly will follow me, I will speak about the record as it is and not as they imagine it to be.
I would like to remind this House that the government of which I am a member came to power some seven years ago. It inherited a backlog of deficit spending and accumulated debt unprecedented in Canada's history. I suspect if you truly check around the world, on a per capita basis there are not too many countries that saw a growth in their debt and deficit to levels that Canada did. Nothing can wish this record of fiscal irresponsibility away.
It is to the credit of this government that instead of trying to wish the problem away, it has taken some firm action to correct it and I might say particularly in the last three years. It is false and irresponsible to insist that one can spend one's way to prosperity. Instead, the government is taking the responsible course of putting our fiscal house in order as the only sure foundation on which to build the strength of Canada, growth and prosperity.
The facts are quite plain. Canada has a $400 billion deficit. It has a federal debt problem today because during the seventies and eighties governments spent
Supply
more on programs, public services and interest than they received in revenues. While the deficit grew, rather than cut back, governments spent even more money.
By 1984-85 the government had a $16.5 billion operating deficit just on programs and operations. Add to that another $22 billion in interest costs on the national debt and we had a deficit of $38.5 billion. The government was spending $1.33 for every $1 in taxes that it took in.
The result of that "spend today, pay tomorrow" policy was to boost the national debt by nearly eightfold in just 10 years. It went from $27 billion in 1974-75 to $206 billion in 1984-85. Unfortunately the spending track that the Government of Canada was on was almost impossible for us to get off. In the last six years the debt has almost doubled to a level of about $400 billion.
Since the Conservative government came to office, it has been following a very consistent plan to increase Canada's economic potential. In fact the previous member who just spoke said that the solution is not increased taxation but an increase in the over-all pie. I can tell you that the government that I am a member of is in fact trying to do exactly that.
We have had to attack the debt challenge on two fronts. First we had to introduce fundamental structural reforms to revitalize the private sector and encourage the growth that makes possible new government revenues. These initiatives include deregulation of key economic sectors, tax reform, privatization of more than 20 Crown corporations, the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and scrapping of the Foreign Investment Review Agency and the National Energy Program. It has provided a more positive investment climate.
The result of these reforms has provided real fiscal benefits. For example no longer are taxpayers footing the bill for de Havilland and Canadair. The spending on those by the end of 1984 had cost the government at least $2.5 billion. Privatization has helped reduce the public payroll by 80,000 in Crown corporation employees. In the post office, government payments this year will be $500 million less than in 1984-85.
In fact I heard members of the NDP, including the Leader of the NDP, speaking a little earlier about minimum corporate tax. I guess what I would ask her is why, when the government introduced the minimum

December 10,1991
Supply
corporate tax in this House, did her party vote against it? In fact that tax is now in place.
We also put in place a thing called a tax on capital. Why is it then that the NDP party and in fact the Liberal Party voted against those two proposals? They talk about fairness in the tax system yet on those two very specific points both opposition parties clearly voted against them.
We also recognize that Canada's debt burden was itself a barrier to economic growth putting pressures on taxes, inflation and ultimately interest rates. That meant further direct action was needed at the source of the debt problem itself, which was federal spending. We took action.
Under the leadership of the Prime Minister, we established a broad program to control spending. We have made absolute cuts in programs wherever possible and applied severe restraint on growth in other areas. The government has completely eliminated programs on home insulation, oil substitution and heavy water plants. As a result, federal energy subsidies today are $2.4 billion less than they were seven years ago.
We have closed military bases. We have cut back payments to VIA Rail. The size of the civil service has been reduced. It has been difficult but we have made those decisions. That discipline has delivered major results. From 1984-85 to 1990-91 growth in federal program spending-that is all spending except interest payments and debt-has been held to just 3.7 per cent a year. That compares with an average annual growth rate of 13.8 per cent in the previous 15 years.
We have gone even further because we have introduced into this House a proposal in the last budget which is now being finalized by the Minister of Finance, which is a spending control act. This will in fact restrict our arms and our ends and the way government spends money for the next five years.
It is important to recognize that two-thirds of the improvement in the operating balance has in fact been accomplished by expenditure control. Revenues account for only one-third of the improvement. As a matter of
fact, government revenues as a share of Gross Domestic Product are no higher than they were in the early 1970s.
Because the government has achieved this operating surplus, the entire increase in the national debt since 1984-85 is due only to compound interest or interest charges on the debt we inherited. The fact is we have to make those interest payments and that means further deficits and still growing debt and the interest charges that debt imposes.
That is why in the February budget there were further measures introduced: first, to hold the deficit to $30.5 billion this year despite the impact of the recession, the agricultural subsidy war and the possible Persian Gulf war expenditures. That was a major accomplishment, in my mind. Second, we plan on getting the deficit down to $25 billion next year for the first time in a decade. We will be setting it on a path where it will continue to fall even further. Third, we plan on eliminating the need for new government borrowings on financial markets by 1994-95. This will be the first time in 25 years that no such borrowings will be necessary by the Government of Canada.
It has been tough and we have got to take some actions. I mentioned we introduced the spending control act which establishes very specific limits on program expenditure growth for the next five years. In fact the finance committee has reviewed that particular spending control act and has made its report.
Nearly all of the increases in program spending over the next two years are concentrated where they are in fact most needed: old age security, unemployment insurance benefits, increases in transfers to lower income provinces and social assistance transfers under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Complimenting the spending control act, we have the debt servicing and reduction account which will ensure that all net revenues of the GST will only be used to service and reduce the debt itself ultimately. That is what Canadians demanded during the GST hearings. That is what they demanded when the GST was put in place. They wanted a guarantee that the government was not going to spend the revenue of the GST on new programs. They have that commitment in the form of legislation from our government.
Finally we established specific inflation targets to get inflation down to less than 2 per cent by the end of 1995. We have seen already that lower inflation is the key to
December 10, 1991

interest rate reduction. The banks prime lending rate is at the lowest level since the early 1970s. Some mortgage rates are lower than they have been since the 1960s. I can vouch for that personally. We purchased our first house in 1970 and in that entire period from 1970 through until today I have never had a mortgage rate as low as I have today. There are results.
In my constituency, which has substantial housing development going on, even in the recession environment, I can tell you that mortgage rates are very important to my constituents. Lower rates have reduced in fact the cost of servicing the debt.
Good economic management means focusing and facing up to the fiscal reality. It does not mean promising silver bullet solutions, lower interest rates at whim, increased government spending that ignores our destructive debt burden or a dollar lower than the market determines that the opposition is trying to sell the Canadians. Those are just snake oil potions. They are all recipes for enduring competitive weakness and national decline.
We have to keep things in perspective as we look ahead to the challenges that we face as Canadians. We have one of the most prosperous countries in the world with an enviable record of wealth, income and job creation. We have the seventh largest economy in the world. We have the second highest standard of living. In other words, we should recognize and build on those strengths. By holding the course of putting our fiscal house in order, our government has chosen the responsible course. This is one that means we can and will be able to build on strength and not weaknesses. Finally I would like to turn to another vital area where the government has proposed ways to strengthen our economic potential. These are the proposals we have made to improve the working of our national economic union. These proposals would strengthen our economy in two important ways.
Before I list those ways, I should point out that in my riding we have discussions going on about the constitutional proposals that are before the country. Many Canadians seem to come out with the standard line: "Would you forget about the Constitution? Would you deal with our economic problems?" Well, those Canadians obviously have not read the proposals to their fullest, because if they truly look at them they will see

that of the 28 proposals out there before Canadians right now, 14 of them deal with the economic issues of this country. That is where we need to make progress, and clearly that is where the government is acting.
I would like to return to my comments about two very specific issues. First we are trying to remove barriers to the free flow of persons, goods, services and capital.
Second, we are facilitating a process of joint decision making by federal and provincial governments on issues where greater co-ordination and harmonization can improve the operation of our economic union. The internal barriers in our domestic market represent a great burden to all Canadians.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association estimates that the cost to the average family of four in Canada is $1,000 a year because of those barriers that exist. Those are internal barriers, provincial trade barriers operating against Canadians.
To deal with that, we have proposed an amendment of the so-called common market clause in the Constitution. It would empower Canadians, both businesses and individuals, to challenge through the courts government practices that create barriers or restrictions to the free flow of people, goods, services and capital within Canada on the basis of provincial or territorial boundaries.
The effect of such constitutional amendment would be clear and simple. It would provide all Canadians with the right to pursue the livelihood of their choice and economic opportunities wherever they choose to do so across our great country. However, a strengthened, competitive economic union will require more than this. It will also require greater co-ordination and harmonization of policies between all levels of government, but particularly between the federal government and the provincial governments.
In the past, federal and provincial governments have had no mechanisms through which they could work together as partners to implement beneficial economic policies. In the absence of such a mechanism, federal-provincial meetings have often seemed to many Canadians as little more than a tug of war because there was no way to take decisions and no need for anyone to stand up and be counted.
We have to do better. What is needed is a joint decision-making mechanism that will allow governments of all levels, working together, to take actions to improve the efficient functioning of our national economy. To this

December 10,1991
Supply
end we have proposed a second amendment to the Constitution.
We are proposing that Parliament be empowered to make laws for the efficient functioning of the economic union with, and I stress only with, the agreement of at least seven provinces with 50 per cent of the population. Because of that provision such a power would not and indeed could not be used as a vehicle for a power grab by the federal government.
Unlike other federal-provincial powers in the Constitution, this power could not be used unless there was an agreement between both levels of government. Its application would be restrictive to co-operative measures that improve the functioning of the Canadian national economic union.
It is important to note that many of our international competitors have strengthened their economic unions by transferring powers to central authorities. Ours is a different approach, with proposals that apply to both levels of government. It is a model that calls for co-operation, not domination.
There is another important point I should add. Not only are our proposals designed to improve the way governments work together, but they also reflect the goal of making the whole economic policy process more open and transparent to the public at large.
Canadian taxpayers and business decision makers have a right to be better informed about policy issues, objectives and constraints. More open and better informed exchanges of views between government and the public is an important foundation to improve our economic performance and our ability to work together. Our government is committed to a course of fiscal progress toward the ultimate goal of debt freedom. Surely everyone in this House would support that goal. It is also important that we keep current economic circumstances in proper perspective. We must not allow an unjustified mood of pessimism about our economic prospects to become a self-fulfilling prophecy. We should also recognize that we have made real progress in getting our financial house in order.
Only by sticking to this responsible course can we ensure and fulfil our future prosperity. That is what good economic management really means.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this extremely important debate, the motion that was introduced by the hon. Leader of the Opposition.
This opposition day motion we are currently debating should be of concern to all Canadians no matter where they live, no matter what their jobs are if they have a job, no matter what their financial circumstances are.
The motion deals with the economy. It deals with the sorry state of affairs this great and wealthy nation currently finds itself in. A little earlier I said this was perhaps the wealthiest and greatest nation in the world. We have been blessed with more resources than any other part of the globe. We count ourselves lucky under God to inhabit this land.
There is a problem and it is not a lack of resources or a lack of ingenuity. The problem is not a lack of caring or wanting by the Canadian public to be productive to have our economy grow and flourish to become more competitive nationally and internationally. The problem comes down to managing that great resource which collectively we all own. That is where the problem is.
This sorry bunch opposite has been in since 1984. I remember 1984. The Prime Minister at that time went around the country with that smirk on his face saying: "Jobs, jobs, jobs". All you had to do was elect Brian Mulroney and his band of Tories and jobs would be everywhere.
In Atlantic Canada he threatened to inflict prosperity upon us. It was a pretty interesting challenge to be taken up.
In 1984 they elected him, figuring maybe he is the best individual to put forward continued liberal type policies of inclusion in the economy, of equalization, of growth of social programs, of growth and increase in our competitiveness and our productivity as a nation.
By the end of 1988 the gig was up. Canadians who had waited with bated breath in every part of this country for prosperity to be inflicted upon them found out there was something being inflicted upon them but it did not start by the letterp. It was not prosperity. It was depression. It was regression. It was recession.
In places like the Atlantic which are the first to slip into recession and the very last to climb out of recession, the same as some parts of western Canada, we waited. By the time the dinner tray got to us there were no crumbs left. In 1988 he knew that his promises of jobs,
December 10, 1991

jobs, jobs was pretty hollow. He and his miracle makers, the mandarins in the back room, and his high priced help from down at the advertising agencies on Bay Street, some even from New York and other places, pulled together a campaign on free trade. Again we were told that the key to the competitiveness and future of the Canadian economy lay with the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. He said: "If you come with us, you will be set free because the borders are going to be opened and there is going to be prosperity. The sun is going to shine and in every garden patch there will be a job again". My colleague says big business bought full-page ads. The Canadian electorate were a little confused. It was not sure, and with friends like big business and full-page ads he managed to squeak in again.
The results are pretty sorry. We are three years down the road now and where is the prosperity? Where is the feeling of Canadians that somehow the greatness of this country has not been spent or misspent by this government? There is a mood in this nation which is foul. We do not even know if we want to stay together any more. Can you imagine? We are blessed. We have been put on this planet, on this soil, in a country that is the richest in the world. Now we are even talking about whether or not we want to stay together, if the French can live with the English, if we all can live with the immigrants and aboriginal Canadians. This did not just crop up. It was not some latent racism and bigotry and urge to self-destruct that we as Canadians always carried. It was planted there by this government.
You start to wonder whether or not you can put bread and butter on the table for your children. It is bread and margarine these days. Nobody can afford butter. You wonder whether or not your kids are going to be able to get a university education. You wonder how you are going to be able to manage if you do qualify for unemployment insurance. Let us look at what government members have done to us. They are so smug on the other side here and when we get up to ask them questions they try to slap us down. They do not want to hear what we have to say, but we are speaking for Canadians.

I want to thank my hon. colleague from Broadview-Greenwood for an appropriate question, particularly at this time of the year. What has happened here is again a matter of confidence. The government has the tools at its disposal. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to stand in this House today to address this very important topic of the economy in Canada.
There are basically four points that I want to make. First, I want to draw a large picture to try to situate Canadians to give them a sense of what is happening within the country. They are not without knowing that the deficit is extremely high. It is in excess of $30 billion. They know that the debt has surpassed $400 billion.
Supply
These are astronomical figures and extremely difficult for most individuals to understand because they do not deal with them on a regular basis.
They know that they have suffered tax increase after tax increase. In fact the number is well over 30.1 believe the count is 34 if we include the goods and services tax. In fact it may be 35 if we include the increased premiums of unemployment insurance.
They see these particular increases and they see the deficit as still very high. The deficit is almost double and they say to themselves: "What is happening? Why are these problems not being resolved?" They recognize as well that when this government came to power the total revenue that it was collecting in taxes was in the neighbourhood of $70 billion.
It is now almost double. It is in excess of $130 billion according to what we project this year. They say: "All of these tax increases, an almost doubling of revenues, and there has been no significant gain with respect to the reduction of the deficit or the debt". They know that there have been until recently extremely high interest rates.
They recognize that if those interest rates had been lower it would have cost us less money to support that debt and to pay the interest. They are not totally sympathetic and that is the kindest way that I can say what has been happening.
They recognize that since June 1989 there have been over 300,000 jobs lost in the manufacturing sector and they worry. They worry about today, tomorrow, themselves, their future and their children's future.
They also know that this country of ours is one of the finest in the world and one where most people from outside our border would like to live. They know it is not only in a serious financial situation but the institutions that we have come to rely upon are really crumbling.

For example in Canada today as we speak-about five million people are poor. Many of them-I believe over a million-are young people, children, and a large majority are women.
Right now we realize that over two million Canadians are on welfare and nearly one and a half million are unemployed. We know very well that the actual number

December 10, 1991
Supply
is much higher because many unemployed people have given up looking.
We know that this year 1.8 million Canadians, almost two million, will have to go to food banks. How can this be in our country? That is what is going on today and it is not at all pleasant. It is shocking. We realize that these
1.8	million Canadians who rely on food banks to eat include about 300,000 children, some very young. It is unimaginable, unacceptable and it frightens people. It makes them lose all confidence.

These same people, as they look at this deteriorating situation which I indicated, are frightened. They are losing confidence in the country, in its institutions and in government. Of course this makes the whole challenge of governing that much more difficult today.
It is not unusual that we should be having serious conflicts throughout the nation. There are conflicts in terms of national unity and conflict in terms of people being unwilling to make accommodations or compromises. Because they are frightened they feel that if they were to do that they would lose even more than they have lost.
They look at the country and they see bankruptcies. I want to quote because I do not want to mislead anyone. There have been more bankruptcies in the first 10 months of this year than in all of last year, which was a record breaking year for both consumer and corporate insolvencies. That was in the province of Manitoba. Between January 1 and November 1 of this year 2,455 bankruptcies were recorded in Manitoba. This includes 331 business failures.
As I travel about my constituency I see vacancy after vacancy. Many of the areas which were once flourishing with small, active, lively, competitive businesses look like disaster areas. That frightens people as well because as they travel back and forth to work and go out and do whatever shopping they can, they see that the situation is not getting better. It is getting worse. It is really getting very bad.
Let me share some personal statistics with which I am dealing in my own constituency. I will use fictitious names to protect the identity of the individual. The first person is Allan who is almost 50 years old. He was removed from his position because it was redundant. He
was in a position of middle management. He has been looking for a job for over a year and has been unable to find anything. He has an excellent work record with superb references.
What about Brian? Brian has a master's degree in public administration. He has not been able to find a full-time job. There are little short jobs and very often he is very poorly remunerated.
What about Charles? Charles has a degree as well, in the area of economics. He has not been able to land a long-term job. If my memory serves me correctly, six months has been the longest job.
What about Donalda who has two degrees? She is a single mother who has not been able to find anything significant. In fact if things continue as they are she will probably have to take a basic entry job which pays a bare minimum wage or slightly over minimum wages.
What about Ernest? Ernest also has a master's degree. He is a new Canadian and full of enthusiasm. What has happened to him? He has been looking for a job for the last several years.
Every one of those individuals, and I can mention some other as well, is a responsible and well educated person. They have excellent skills but they simply cannot get jobs. I have not mentioned the Pauls and the Janices. These are the people who have journeyman papers and a number of trades who have lost their jobs and would have to take roughly half of what they earned if they can get a job. There are many of those people out there as well.
There were 2,000 jobs lost during the last 10 years in the CNR as I mentioned in this House this week. I think it was 1,000 during the last three years. They say: "What is happening to my province? What is happening to my country? What is happening to my city?"
They look at VIA Rail which was decimated with almost 3,000 lost jobs that were never to return. They look at Route Canada which was a trucking firm that went bankrupt a number of years ago and over 1,900 people were just left hanging. Nothing has been done for them. They look at ITEM, the company that was supposed to help small businesses. We do not have the full story there, but we know that it is less than totally pleasant. It did not work out at all. It left people hanging,
December 10, 1991

people who had invested a lot of their time and a lot of their money.
They look at news stories such as the one yesterday about the port of Churchill possibly closing. They saw the headline of just a couple of days ago about the loss of additional jobs at CNR. They look at the cuts in Air Canada and Canadian Airlines International Limited. They wonder when this is going to stop.
What has the government done? It could have invested more in education, but it will have cut $10 billion in education between 1986 and 1995.
In training and retraining there are fewer dollars. We need more training and retraining. In research and development it was going to invest twice as much. What has happened? It slid. It is much less than what it was. I could go on and on.
We need an election. We really need to have the Canadian people say: "This is what we want with this particular program". We need to look at policies such as a lower dollar. We need to look at whatever it is we can do to get Canadians back to work.
I would like to say that if we could make one decision right now, it would be to permit those people with credit cards to have lower rates at this time. I am sure it would help the small business people who are struggling to make it over the Christmas holiday. If it does not work out during the next couple of weeks, they are going to be a lot more bankruptcies.

Mr. Speaker, you caught me off guard. I thought for sure we would have some questions and answers from the other side.
The motion before us today is certainly a serious one. I think it is very important that Canadians have a chance to hear us debate it today in the House of Commons. There is no question that the Canadian economy is hurting, that we are in the midst of a recession, and that we do have a million plus unemployed in this country.
I think what we have to do is not only talk about Canada, but focus on where we are in relation to the rest of the world. Canada is not alone in this thing. None of us in this House enjoys listening to or looking at some of
Supply
the stats that have been thrown around here this morning. Some were quite accurate and some were misleading.
Most of us would agree that we have a million plus unemployed and it is not a nice thing to see when we go back into our ridings. All of us are affected. This unemployment knows no political boundaries. Whether you are NDP, Liberal or Conservative, we are all affected in our individual ridings, neighbourhoods and our individual families. It is not an easy thing to see at this time of year.
As I mentioned at the outset we are not alone in this thing. That is what we have to focus on in this debate today. Canada is moving out of the recession. There are some veiy strong indicators that we are effectively moving out of the recession. There is a long way to go. We admit that but we are moving out of it.
Much of the emphasis today has been on Canada versus the U.S. and the free trade agreement in relation to the U.S. Let us examine the U.S. economy for a minute. Let us take a look at what is going right or what is going wrong with that economy. The United States has monumental problems. When we talk about job losses in Canada, we can talk about a million plus jobs lost and we will accept those figures.
As I mentioned earlier, they are not easy figures to accept, but we will accept them.
South of us in the United States there is unemployment at this very moment ranging, depending on whose figure you want to believe, from 10 million to 12 million. The U.S. has its problems too.
It is interesting to note that we are doing some things in this country about our position. We know we have to get some of the fundamentals right to move beyond where we are this very day.
Some of those fundamentals that we believe are very necessary to move out of recession to a period of recovery and growth I think we have the right concept of and we are doing the things that we have to do versus the United States which refuses to look at the real structural problems within its economy.
We have taken some of those hard decisions in the last couple of years, many hard decisions. Those are not easy ones to go back home and defend, but we have nonetheless taken those.

December 10,1991
Supply
One of the serious problems that we faced in 1984 when we took office was a mounting debt, a crippling debt load, and one that was bound to get us into the kinds of difficulties we are in now.
Take a look at 1984. The percentage of debt in relation to Gross Domestic Product was running at a rate of 8.7 per cent. Take a look at it today. Today that number has almost been cut in half. It is in the area of 4.6 per cent in relation to Gross Domestic Product. That is the real measure of what we have done about the debt because the Canadian economy has grown but our ability to fight that debt in relation to the growth in the economy has been very successful. No one argues that, particularly international investors when they look at this country and can measure what we have done.
Politically it has not been easy. If you want to poke fun at our standings in the polls, they are higher than the interest rates today. A couple of years ago maybe we could have argued that they were not, but they are now.
I think the real truth of what is happening to the Canadian economy can be measured in the international investment world, the investment markets. We are doing the right things, although they are tough politically.
The figure of 4.6 per cent, the figure of debt in relation to Gross Domestic Product, is going to drop to less than 1 per cent by 1995. If our projections are right, it will come down in the order of about .7 per cent, less than 1 per cent. That will be the year that we will also start to pay down the debt. If it is not that year, it will be close to it. We will be in what we call a zero borrowing position. We can start really paying down that debt.
Another difficulty we inherited on this side of the House in 1984 was that our operating balance was out of whack. The cost of programs before paying interest was something in the order of $16 billion more than revenue. We changed that around. Now we have a $12 billion surplus on that operating balance and that operating account.
That was the thing which restricted us from paying down the debt. All political arguments aside, if you look at the debt we inherited, which was $200 billion plus in 1984, what we have today when we look at the accumulated debt of approximately $390 billion is accumulated interest on that debt because the structural deficit we
inherited restricted us from paying down the dollar amount of that debt. We are simply paying interest on it.
We know how much that interest is gobbling up in terms of government revenues today.
Canadians are probably paying too much in taxes and 35 cents out of every dollar simply pays interest on the debt.
It is crazy. It is a crazy position for a government to get into. How did we allow ourselves to get into that position? Again, it is the old trick that I usually pull back in the riding. I pull the pen out of the pocket. It is interesting that I have a red pen here because those red numbers were simply created in those years leading up to 1984 when politicians went back home to their ridings and simply wrote the cheque knowing full well the money was not here to pay for it.
We did not have the money to pay the bills. We had to borrow it. We went on that destructive course and we had been on it for many years.
This is the first government in the last 30 years that has decided we cannot go on that destructive course. That 35 cents you are sending to Ottawa to pay the debt is money that is wasted.
Just imagine the types of programs we could have today if 35 cents of our dollar were not simply going to pay interest on the debt. It is wasted money. It is money that cannot be used for health care programs. It cannot be used for housing programs. It is simply money that is wasted. It is going to the bond holders who are reaping the rewards of this.
Talk about irony. The people who need the money the least are the ones who gain in a system laden with debt. Canada has done what very few western countries have done in the last 10, 20, 30 years. Canada has faced reality and is going back to square one.
An editorial in The Globe and Mail dated November 7, 1991 says it all. Talking about the U.S., the headline is "A wake-up call for George Bush". What it is saying is simply that the United States of America has refused to come to grips with its overspending as we have in Canada. When I mentioned those Gross Domestic Product figures in relation to debt, our position is much
December 10, 1991

more favourable now than it was seven years ago, eight years ago, ten years ago.
Our position is on a projectile and you can see light at the end of the tunnel. The American position is straight up. Politically it does not want to deal with it. Politically when you deal with debts and deficits there is a price to be paid on the other end. When you go back into your respective neighbourhoods without those programs and the cheques in your pockets to do the types of things that make you popular in your ridings, they are not there.
The U.S. has not come to grips with that. It has its eye on the 1992 election, but it does not want to deal with the truth. It wants to continue to spend by borrowing from future generations.
We are not going to do that any more in this country. That is one of the reasons why we are bringing in, as a government, a proposed spending control act. At this point it is proposed because it has not been laid before the House, so to speak.
What it is saying is simply that we are going to put restrictions on the Government of Canada to spend the taxpayers' money. We know the future of this country can only be secured when we erase that burden of debt under which we are operating today. We are going to do it.
Some of the arguments that we have heard in this House this morning were in relation to the free trade agreement. I want to dismiss some of those. They are not painting an accurate picture at all.
The trade agreement with the United States is working. It is not perfect but it is working. I want to give some statistics that I will back up any day of the week, any place.
Our exports to the United States in the first two years since the free trade agreement have increased by $8 billion. Since the free trade agreement, our trade surplus with the United States has gone up by about $3 billion. Between 1988 and 1990 Canada went from a net direct investment outflow of $2.5 billion to a net direct investment inflow of $5.1 billion for a net turn around of $7.6 billion.
Those are good figures, believable figures. It is working. In August of this year Statistics Canada announced that our exports to the U.S. were at an all-time high.
Supply
The FTA has been good for Canada. It has been very positive for Canada.
In this House the opposition is quite famous for coming in with names of companies, fictitious or otherwise, that have abandoned Canada as a place to invest. I want to go through some of the companies that have left the United States and have come to Canada with their money, with their investments. Let us go through some of these.
Canadian Thermos Products has closed plants in the United States and come to Canada as a good place to invest. Gandalf Technologies in Nepean is a U.S. company that moved to Canada. Heron Cable of Waterloo, Ontario left the U.S. and came to Canada. Hughes Aircraft Company located in Midland, Ontario left the U.S. and came to Canada.
There are others such as Inter-City Products Corporation, Brantford, Ontario; Kodak Canada Limited; Keep-Rite Incorporated of Brantford, Ontario; Sault Star Seamless Cylinder Co. of Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario; J. L. DeBall Ltd. of Montreal; Polymer International, now in Nova Scotia; a litany of companies because Canada is a good place to invest.
International investors are recognizing that simply because of what we are doing. We are erasing that burden of debt and attracting international investors to this country.
One of the arguments they make on the other side is that the Canadian dollar is too high. Maybe it is too high. We do not argue that but world markets determine the value of the Canadian dollar. The world markets and investors are telling Canadians that we have a good country and it is a good place to invest. The level of the Canadian dollar is merely a reflection of what we are doing; building a strong country with a strong economy. More important, we are getting the fundamentals right. We are getting them down into the area in which investors can live with them, especially regarding inflation.
What we want to achieve is an economy in which inflation is as low as it can possibly get. We are achieving that. We also want to have an economy in which we have what we call price stability. We are achieving that. Those are the types of things that attract investment into a country. Those are the types of things that have attracted

December 10, 1991
those companies that I just mentioned into Canada. We are doing those types of things.
We are also talking about job stability. Let us talk about the GST. The opposition loves to talk about that. We brought in a change to the old manufacturers' sales tax in this country to help manufacturing. That is what it is doing. It is helping manufacturing. It is bringing foreign investment into this country and doing what we said it would do.
If the opposition wants to argue on the political merits of the GST and the negative impact it has on our standings in the polls, I will support that 100 per cent. It is doing the tough things but doing them for the right reasons, and the right reasons are simply to gear up the Canadian economy so we can compete in the 1990s and into the turn of the century, doing the types of things that we were elected to do. We were not elected to simply stay in office and do the easy things. We were elected to make the tough decisions for the benefit of all Canadians.
Our economic policies are working. When the Canadian people go to the polls in 1993 they will have a chance to reflect and they will say we have done the right things, the tough things, and they will be willing to re-elect us.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN ECONOMIC SITUATION
speechtext: It being two o'clock p.m., the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, each year governments in Europe and North America subsidize consumers through programs to assist farmers that produce food at a loss.
Canada has developed a system of supply management which makes a great deal of sense to producers, processors and consumers with minimal support from the Canadian Treasury.
There has been a great deal of encouragement and support throughout Canada for the position that the
federal government has taken at the GATT negotiations to see article XI:2(c)(i) strengthened and clarified.
Better access to world-wide markets, clear and fair rules on countervailing duties and rules to prevent the abuse of health and sanitary reasons as disguised trade barriers are important.
It is imperative if agriculture is to survive in Canada that we have a more stable environment for our domestic and export producers.
I urge all members of Parliament to support the government in order to ensure success in Canada's position during these last minute negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, Air Canada has failed to ensure that the federal policy relating to employment contracts of airport screening personnel was respected at the Halifax International Airport.
The federal policy was that the turnover of these workers would be reduced through improvement and protection of wages and benefits. Transport Canada was supposed to ensure job security and wage benefits for the workers during turnover. It did not.
Those workers have lost their wages and they have lost their jobs. As of last week, workers with as much as nine years of experience had not been offered seniority by the new screening firm.
There were 30 employees at Walker Security. I therefore call upon the government to instruct Air Canada to review the contract with the new security firm. If it finds that the firm has abrogated the commitment that it made to both Air Canada and the workers, it should declare the contract void and sit down to ensure that we have fairness to those employees.
These people have been abandoned by Transport Canada, and they have been abandoned by this government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to remind all hon. members that today is a very significant occasion in Canada and throughout the world. It is International Human Rights Day, and the 43rd
December 10, 1991

anniversary of the United Nations adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
The world has made gigantic steps. However, violations of human rights are still reported every day. That is why we must continue in partnership with other nations our efforts to ensure progress toward a world free of injustice, discrimination and prejudice.
Today, the Nobel Peace Prize will be awarded to Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, a founder of Myanmar's National League for Democracy, a courageous woman, currently under house arrest for her beliefs. All members of the Subcommittee on Development and Human Rights of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade congratulate her and call for her immediate release.
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the NDP government in British Columbia is responding to the recommendations of the First Nations task force report on land claims.
Since my first days in the B.C. legislature almost 18 years ago, I have been urging that land claims be settled in my province on the basis of aboriginal rights and title.
Now that we finally have a government in British Columbia willing to do so, the federal minister of Indian Affairs is throwing up another road-block.
By threatening to stall negotiations with First Nations until the province accepts his preconditions on costsharing, the minister appears not to want to sit down with aboriginal people at all.
I commend Mike Harcourt's, aboriginal affairs minister Andrew Petter, and the NDP government for their historic, precedent setting commitment to settling the outstanding claims of First Nations in B.C.
I call on the minister of Indian Affairs to dismantle his road-block, drop the preconditions he has placed on negotiations with the First Nations, and get on to negotiating an honourable land claim settlement in British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, as my colleague from St. Albert just said in English, I would like to remind this House that December 10 has been declared International Human Rights Day and today is the 43rd anniversary of the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights by the United Nations.
Exactly 43 years ago, the UN General Assembly adopted this universal declaration, this document which was to give all people everywhere the same basic rights and freedoms. This does not mean that injustice and intolerance have completely disappeared from the face of the earth. Unfortunately in some countries these rights and freedoms are not respected. Canada has adopted its own Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but much remains to be done. We want to give all Canadians, without exception, a chance to participate fully in our society.
International Human Rights Day is an opportunity to reflect but also to act. We should take this opportunity to ask ourselves how we as Canadians can build a fairer, more tolerant country, a country where everyone can contribute to the best of their ability.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday, once again Canadians recalled the Montreal massacre, an event that focuses attention every December 6 on the issue of violence against women. Today and every day, women and children see their lives and families shattered by violence, violence that governments have done little to prevent or punish.
I call upon members of this House and all other legislatures in this country to look to their statutes and public programs for ways to control the menace that lurks in so many Canadian homes. Our laws must be made more effective, not just in words but in practice. Shelters only deal with the consequences of violence. Society must start to deal with the causes.

December 10, 1991
Children and mothers across the land are looking to their legislators for protection. Parliament must not fail them again.

Mr. Speaker, I stand today to endorse the objective of national standards testing in education as proposed by the provincial governments at their meeting in Toronto yesterday.
As we all know, the future of our country will depend upon the ability to compete. However, this ability to compete is not attainable without a properly educated society.
In Canada today the inability to move east to west or west to east to provide for one's self and create a stronger economy is restricted by the lack of national education standards. I hope now that the business community and the political community are working together to set national standards that the educational community will be a very important part of this new strategy.
I congratulate all of the provincial governments for their efforts in reaching this agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take this opportunity to commend approximately 200 Prince Edward Island fishermen who participated in the 11th annual convention and seminar at the Prince Edward Island Fishermen's Association this past weekend.
It was unfortunate that the federal minister of fisheries was unable to attend the event because he missed a great opportunity to listen to the concerns, views and possible solutions put forward by Prince Edward Island fishermen.
The fishing industry employs approximately 10 per cent of our work force in Prince Edward Island. In 1989 it contributed $226 million to our provincial economy.
Among the many issues discussed, perhaps the most serious issue remains the government's reluctance to return to a standard minimum lobster carapace size of
2.5	inches for all three designated areas on the Island.
I look forward to receiving copies of the resolutions passed which I hope to share with this House at the earliest opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the unfair treatment Serbian people are receiving from the highest levels of our parliamentary system. There are more than 100,000 Serbs in Canada, and Serbia has always been Canada's ally: Furthermore, the Serbs were one of the groups that suffered most during the two last wars in which they lost almost a third of their population.
Today these people have a right to be treated fairly in the House of Commons. In fact, its most basic rights as a society have not been recognized, although today, it remains the first victim of the surge in fascism in Europe. It seems that people in certain Canadian political circles are playing a most unfortunate role in the present crisis in Yugoslavia. One would hope that in this country all parties concerned would at least have the decency to look at both sides of the story.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in celebration with six northwestern Ontario aboriginal communities which finally, after decades of neglect, will now receive a secure land base and the funds necessary to develop water and sewage services, decent housing, community facilities, not to mention the chance for economic improvements.
As my colleague Bud Wildman, Ontario minister of native affairs, said yesterday: "We are taking the first
December 10, 1991

step toward ensuring that six communities in the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation will have a brighter and healthier future".
It is an historic first step to the people of the First Nations of Kee-Way-Win, McDowell Lake, New Slate Falls, Saugeen, Aroland and Wawakapewin. My congratulations and best wishes.
To the Government of Ontario: Thanks for providing the leadership to solve this dispute so long in occurring.
To the federal government: What took you so long?
Let us use this decision to move forward toward resolving all of the outstanding aboriginal issues. It is our responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, for decades the main highway entrance to Nova Scotia has provided the most unique welcome of any province.
With a huge flower garden and information kiosks describing the provincial attractions, all tourists have been made at home right away.
Now, with the new highway about to bypass this entrance, it is important that tourism groups unite with the province to rearrange and rebuild this unique welcoming facility. The Amherst and area Development Commission has spearheaded the drive to create an even more impressive display than ever before.
The proposal includes replacing the Bluenose II at the site where it will be the first impression that tourists have as they enter the province and their last impression as they leave the province.
The Bluenose II will soon be retired and the border site provides the best possible location where virtually all visitors will have the opportunity to see the symbol of our Nova Scotia heritage and know that they have arrived at a unique province.
I call on the tourism ministry, the province, the federal government and all interested parties to work closely to achieve this goal of re-establishing this entrance to Nova Scotia.

subtopic: CANADA EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ADVISORY COUNCIL
CANADA EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council, established in 1977, was mandated to provide the government with independent advice on policy issues.
In recent years the council has recommended, among other things, a full employment policy, a regional employment strategy, adjustment programs for older workers and opposed cutbacks in unemployment insurance. In most cases the government has totally ignored this advice.
Now there is serious concern that the government will close the council down. Currently there are five vacancies on the council which have not been filled, including the chairperson and one vice-chairperson.
What are the government's plans with respect to this independent, broadly based, private sector advisory council? Can the government not take advice which says it is wrong on several matters? Is this another example of the government suppressing legitimate dissent?
What is the future of the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council?

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is committed to a safer environment.
As part of the green plan, our government will improve the ability of Canadians to predict and warn about weather emergencies. Each year some 150 Canadians die from the direct effects of severe weather. Many others are affected by floods and automobile accidents caused by poor weather.
Under this $40 million program, weather emergencies and emergency surveillance systems will be upgraded and the public will be made more aware of natural disasters and how we can respond to them.
Doppler radars already in place in Edmonton and Toronto will also be installed in Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec to give more advance notice of tornadoes. A more accurate computer model will be developed to improve Canada's ability to track clouds of

December 10, 1991
nuclear fall-out, volcanic eruptions and major toxic gas releases.
The weather radio network, which already includes more than 100 transmitters, will be expanded further and upgraded, and special emergency television messages will warn of impending floods and of iceberg movements.
Let us all work together for a safer environment for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, this government's high tax, high dollar, free trade induced recession is continuing to cost Canadian workers their jobs.
In my riding of Kootenay West-Revelstoke the following plant closures last year contributed to an unemployment rate of 13.9 per cent.
Lost are 95 high-tech jobs moved to the U.S. due to closure of Johnson-Matthey in Trail; 167 woods product jobs permanently lost due to closures: YMIR Forest Products, Koala Timber, L & W Sawmills, Poplar Cedar, Shelly Cedar, and Eaglewood Firewood.
Many more have been laid off: 240 from Westar Timber in Castelgar; 50 more from Treminco Resources Mine shutdown at Sandon; 130 more at Kalesnikoff Lumber, Kootenay Valley Sawmills and Slocan Forest Products; 100 more from shutdowns at Columbia River Shake and Shingle; and at least 200 loggers are out of work as a result of all this carnage. I and my constituents urge the Prime Minister and his finance minister to open their eyes and see the damage they are causing.
There are none so blind as those who will not see.
My message is this: Stop, look and listen to unemployed Canadians. Shape up or ship out.

Mr. Speaker, it is most important that we cling to the symbols which unite us and pay tribute to those who have served their country. Like all other Canadians, I commended and
applauded the Minister of Veterans Affairs last spring when he announced that a medal was finally being struck and awarded to those members of our Armed Forces who so valiantly served in the Korean war some 40 years ago.
It was nice to see a few of the medals presented in early November in a ceremony with the Governor General, but does the minister realize the time it is taking to process the applications for the medals and does he also realize that these medals are slated to be mailed out rather than be presented in any formal fashion to the recipients?
Mr. Speaker, the hypocrisy of it all. How can this government mail out medals of honour?
I call on the government to provide the persons who earned these medals with a more dignified presentation than is being planned at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians can be proud of the substantial progress which has been made on the green plan as 80 per cent of first year program targets will be met by the end of the fiscal year.
Canadians in all regions will benefit from important initiatives which range from the Canada-U.S. air quality accord to the $275 million Indian health and water initiative.
Through the $100 million Arctic environmental strategy, northern communities and non-governmental organizations will be assisted to take local action on important environmental issues.
We are also expending some $100 million to help clean up the Fraser River and to return salmon populations to historical levels.
The $10 million Atlantic coast action program to restore harbours and coastal areas will fund programs run by a cross-section of community residents along with government, industry and business representatives.
In summation, we are making good progress in our stated goal to integrate environmental protection and economic development. We are improving the manner in which decisions are made and that is the best news of all.
December 10, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance and some of his fellow ministers from the province of Quebec met with businessmen and union leaders in Montreal and according to the press reports the meeting was not a success.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance why he will not admit that Montreal businessmen and Montreal union leaders were right when they said it was useless for our bank rate to be 3 per cent higher than the bank rate in the U.S. Why did the government not take the necessary action to set the Canadian dollar at a level that would allow plants that are now closed in the Montreal area to start up again?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hate to disappoint the hon. Leader of the Opposition, but my colleagues and I had a very productive and constructive meeting with the Quebec business community. They acknowledge the fact that interest rates are the lowest they have been in 18 years. We have the third lowest interest rates in the world, next to the United States and Japan. The spread the hon. member speaks of is the spread between the Bank of Canada rate and the Fed in the United States.
As I said in the House this morning, people do not borrow from the Fed and they do not borrow from the Bank of Canada. They borrow from the commercial banks and the differential is about one-half of one per cent. Our prime rate in Canada is 8 per cent. The prime rate in the United States is 7.5 per cent. That is a tremendous record.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as he has done for the last few weeks, this morning the minister told Canadians that he thinks the recession is over.
Oral Questions
He should know that, for example, last month housing starts were down 13 per cent. That was one sector we were led to believe was doing better and it was 13 per cent below what it was a year ago.
I want to ask the minister why he is not recognizing the fact that we are not out of the recession and why he keeps trying to defend the indefensible, the budget of his predecessor, and why he is not coming out with his own budget so we have a chance to create some hope for Canadians at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is true that housing starts declined somewhat in November over October, but I remind the hon. member that housing starts in the month of October reached 204,000, the highest in 17 months.
It would be very unusual to maintain that kind of growth. I can tell the hon. member that housing starts have strengthened. They come in at 178,000 units but obviously housing being an interest sensitive sector, and given the fact that in the third quarter it was recorded that investment in residential housing had increased by
17.2	per cent, I think those are positive indicators for the housing industry and I agree with the hon. member.
As the housing industry is stimulated that has a very major impact upon the total economy of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be useful if the minister were more realistic and looked at what is happening.
Last week, for example, we learned that the Town and Country clothing chain will close 162 stores across Canada. Today the Ayres chain declared that it will close 60 stores across Canada. It is not waiting for Christmas; it is moving right away.
They all have the same reasons: high dollar, high interest rate, cross-border shopping, GST, and a terrible economic situation.
I ask the minister again: Why does he try to defend a budget that has been a complete failure and why does he not introduce a new budget on his own that might make more sense than the one presented by his colleague to his left?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would much rather

December 10, 1991
Oral Questions
follow the advice of the former Minister of Finance than the track record of the Leader of the Opposition, which is pretty dismal.
I put a few things on the record this morning. For example, his first budget was over the target by 70 per cent. The second budget was over its target by 30 per cent in terms of the deficit. In those days when he was President of the Treasury Board he talked about a 16 per cent increase in program expenditures as restraint. Some restraint.
That is not to take away from the seriousness of the question that the hon. member raised. Obviously, and I want to point out to the hon. member, this government does not have a high interest rate policy. With the interest being the lowest in 18 years, that is far from being a high interest rate policy.
Clearly our aim and objective is to get the basics right, the fundamentals right, and bring about a decline in the inflationaiy pressures. That will bring down interest rates, as it has, and that will provide the climate for sustainable growth and price stability.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday the Prime Minister said that poverty was decreasing in Newfoundland. Well, he was wrong.
In Newfoundland alone the welfare roll is increasing at the rate of 2,000 people a month and is at record highs. When the Prime Minister said poverty was decreasing he must have been in Disneyland, not Newfoundland. The ostrich approach may make the government feel good, but it does not put food on the table.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister what he can tell a four-year old Newfoundland child lined up at the food bank that can give him some hope this Christmas.

Mr. Speaker, I will not comment on the frivolous conclusion of my hon. friend's question, but with regard to the information raised yesterday I simply indicated, and I think the statistics will bear it out, and I am speaking
from memory, that unemployment in Newfoundland is down in the neighbourhood of 6 per cent from where we inherited it in 1984. It is still too high. It was 23.5 per cent when the Liberals left office. It is down to 18.1 per cent, I believe, today.
We are working. Some 25,000 new jobs have been created in Newfoundland in the last six years as opposed to 1,000 jobs that were lost in the period from 1980 to 1984.
Hibernia is creating some 35,000 new jobs and some 3,500 permanent jobs. Premier Wells I think agreed yesterday-you may want to check with him-that the general fiscal and financial approach of the Government of Canada is one that he generally supports. He is very pleased with what we have done with Hibernia and other economic initiatives and he believes that the co-operation between the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador will bring prosperity to that province.

Mr. Speaker, my question about the four-year old boy who will end up eating at a food bank this Christmas is not a joke. It is the truth. In Montreal alone 50,000 children will eat at food banks this Christmas. That being the case, why does the government and why do the Prime Minister and his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, keep claiming that poverty has not increased, while they know perfectly well the unemployment rate and the welfare rate are going up, not down?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is wrong again. No one can ignore the social problems we have in this country today. In Quebec we have some serious problems, for instance in East Montreal and a number of areas in eastern Quebec, and there are also problems in the Atlantic region and other parts of this country. There will always be too many cases of poverty and too many cases where the children of this country are involved. But the government has done a great deal. And I believe that very soon the Minister of National Health and Welfare will announce a number of major initiatives to provide
December 10, 1991

greater security for children who are affected by poverty and other social problems.
That being said, I think we should realize that the real wealth of a nation is created by the private sector, not by governments with deficits. And the private sector will create wealth if interest rates go down. Today, however, interest rates are at their lowest levels in 18 years and the inflation rate is at its lowest level in 21 years. Those are signs that should encourage, not discourage the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Many Canadians were astonished when they heard on September 30 this year that the democratically elected president of Haiti, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, had been toppled by a coup d'etat. Canada has now frozen $20 million in aid, of which $10 million was earmarked for non-governmental organizations.
We are in favour of economic sanctions against the military dictatorship, but the situation of the poor who have no shelter and no food is appalling. Will the government reinstate the assistance channelled through NGOs?

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government supports President Aristide and all efforts to help the president resume his democratic duties in Port-au-Prince. We also support the embargo ordered by the Organization of American States. Although it is unfortunate that the embargo is causing serious problems for a broad segment of the population, I believe that President Aristide's position is that the people of Haiti prefer this kind of temporary problem to the loss of democracy. He believes that these initiatives on the part of the Canadian government are helping to restore democracy in Haiti. That is why we intend to persevere in our efforts in this respect.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. I gather that means that the government will not be assisting the Red Cross and other organizations which have asked for additional aid in order to assist those people in Haiti who are suffering.
My question for the Prime Minister on another subject however is that he was very careful on another international matter regarding the break-up of the Soviet
Oral Questions
Union and careful in Canada's response to this extremely complex and volatile matter. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, however, was not quite so cautious in her comments about the Slavic commonwealth. She said: "The Soviet Union is evolving into a new format and the changes we see are positive".
I would ask the Prime Minister if he would tell us today if he agrees that recent developments are positive, and will he let the House know if this is the message that he has conveyed to Mikhail Gorbachev?

Mr. Speaker, I was away yesterday, but I looked at the transcript and I am told that the minister indicated that it was a positive sign that the three republics wish to work together. That of course is by any standards a positive sign.
Our concerns-and I think they are probably shared by my hon. friend- in respect of the Soviet Union are political stability in the former U.S.S.R., because there is general agreement that it is in an evolving state, on terms that would be agreed to. We have deep concerns, as I expressed in the House the other day, about the deployment, use and control of nuclear weapons on the sods of many of the republics. We have concerns about food shortages, shortages of medicines this winter and the devastation that may inflict upon the Soviet people. We have concerns that we have expressed about minorities and borders so as to ensure that the situation in the Soviet Union does not disintegrate into the catastrophe that has now engulfed Yugoslavia.
We are proceeding with caution. We are proceeding with great care because we would like to have a constructive influence, if we can, on the development of matters in the Soviet Union. To that end we will consult with parties in the House and we will try to take the most constructive attitude possible.

I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister has outlined a number of concerns that I think many Canadians and many people throughout the world have, while certainly supporting co-operation among newly independent states.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister a specific question about one of the issues he himself raised. In the three new Soviet states there are 8,911 nuclear warheads

December 10,1991
Oral Questions
pointed toward North America and Europe. Yesterday there were conflicting statements from leaders in the three new Soviet republics regarding control of that arsenal.
The Prime Minister said that he is concerned, but I would like to ask him what action he has taken to convey that concern to the leaders of these new republics, and will he ask them to provide a specific plan for the control, non-proliferation and eventual elimination of this nuclear arsenal?

Mr. Speaker, I think that the position that we have adopted and conveyed to President Gorbachev personally and to the various ministers representing appropriate republics can be summarized in the communication that we conveyed to the President of Ukraine when we recognized the independence of Ukraine.
We recognized independence for Ukraine, but we began a process of negotiating diplomatic recognition pursuant to four or five important criteria, including some that have just been raised by my hon. friend. We have senior officials in Kiev doing that with a republic whose independence we have recognized. We will no doubt proceed in a similar fashion under analogous circumstances because the problems in large measure remain the same in the various republics.
I think that the precedent that the Government of Canada has established and laid down in regard to Ukraine can be looked upon for guidance in regard to the evolution of the other Soviet republics.
I should advise the House that I am going to break with our recent practice and I think the House will agree with the reason for doing so at this moment.
I wish to draw the attention of the House to the presence in our gallery of His Excellency Mr. Jean-Bertrand Aristide, President of Haiti.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance in his answer to the Leader of the
Official Opposition acknowledged the figures that were released by CMHC, indicating that housing starts had plunged by 13 per cent.
The Minister of Finance has several proposals made by the housing industry, such as the Canadian Real Estate Association proposal dealing with RRSPs and the 5 per cent down payment for home buyers.
When will the government take action on these proposals and introduce pro-active policies to kick-start the housing industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just to reiterate, the housing starts have been strong: 204,000 housing starts in the month of October. That was the highest in 17 months. I acknowledge as I indicated in an earlier answer that anything that would stimulate the housing industry further still certainly has a very major spinoff effect upon the total economy.
The two proposals to which the hon. member has referred are proposals that I am looking at very carefully with my colleague, the Minister of Public Works and minister in charge of CMHC. Hopefully we will be able to come up with some positive actions on those fronts. I hope to be in a position to announce the results of that review in the not too distant future.

Mr. Speaker, this government should start walking down Main Street, Canada, and see the real world out there. According to CMHC, federal housing programs are not reaching over 1.25 million households that are in need of assistance, and yet this government keeps slashing dollars and programs. This is unacceptable, uncaring and irresponsible.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance when this government will honour its commitments and its responsibilities and restore the funding to build affordable housing units and co-operative units in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):

There has been $116 million put into an increase in housing assistance.
December 10, 1991

I think the hon. member should realize that people in Canada are asking: Do you want to raise taxes to do that? Should this government act responsibly? We say yes, we should, and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Prime Minister who, after meeting with Premier Wells yesterday, undertook to his great credit to reassess the fishery reforms announced last week by his Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, a hare-brained scheme if ever I saw one and whose only motive must have been to put Atlantic fishermen at each other's throats.

Well, if it is not what the press says you can blame them, not me. I apologize, Roger. They are always right. I am sorry.

-said that every fisherman or plant worker who qualifies for assistance under the Fisheries Assis-

tance Program will get that assistance or "My name is not John Carnell Crosbie".

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to say we appreciate President Aristide's presence here, but we would prefer to see him in Haiti's Parliament, right now.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Prime Minister concerning the historic and serious developments taking place in the former republics of the Soviet Union.
The secretary of state said yesterday that she welcomed these as a positive development. The Prime Minister today is saying that we are now proceeding with caution.
I wonder if the Prime Minister could tell us what it is that Canada is going to do and how are we going to proceed. Are we in fact withdrawing recognition from the present apparatus of the Soviet government, headed by President Gorbachev? Will we be extending recognition to the so-called new commonwealth? Will we be starting discussions to establish diplomatic relations with all the other republics of the former Soviet Union?
Perhaps the Prime Minister could tell us exactly what we are going to do.

Mr. Speaker, I indicated that in response to another question. I understand that the minister yesterday said that it was a positive sign that the three republics wished to work together. Obviously anything that brings greater stability to the region is veiy much a positive sign.
When I was in St. John's yesterday and before the minister spoke, I believe, I indicated that the policy of the Government of Canada was that we would wait for
December 10, 1991

President Gorbachev's speech which he delivered later that day and that we would look at this with a great deal of caution because of the four or five concerns that I mentioned to the leader of the NDP, particularly the deployment and control of nuclear weapons on the soil of a number of these republics.
As we speak, events are taking place. We are being briefed on a very regular basis by our ambassador, our representatives in Kiev and elsewhere. We are monitoring it very, very closely so that the policy of the Government of Canada will become one that is helpful and constructive in pursuance of the four or five criteria I laid out both in the question of Ukraine and in response to the Leader of the NDP today.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. One concern the Prime Minister did not raise in his early remarks was the arrangements made with the former Soviet government with wheat sales and over $2 billion worth of credit.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister specifically: Are we continuing to send food aid to the various republics of the Soviet Union? If so, under what kind of credit arrangements and what kind of repayment arrangements will we be making? Will those simply be held in abeyance? Will we continue that kind of important humanitarian aid during these very critical winter months?

Mr. Speaker, I wrote to President Gorbachev a few days ago when we decided our course in regard to Ukraine. I conveyed to him the view of the Government of Canada, that we would be helpful to him as he grappled with these various problems my hon. friend has just raised in regard to foodstuffs, medicines and so on, particularly with the encroaching winter.
With regard to grain sales, I would have to check. But my recollection is that in the last major grain sale that was concluded by the Government of Canada through the Canadian Wheat Board, we received a counter-signature from the Republic of Russia. The Minister of Agriculture signals that is correct. We had the negotiations that took place in the normal course, but we asked for a further guarantee, and we obtained it.

Will the Prime Minister today demand an independent objective UN commission of inquiry into the East Timorese killings?
